# How to use this guide

Pharmacotherapeutics (ER20-24T) is a second-year D.Pharm subject of 75 theory hours, with a linked practical, ER20-24P (25 hours). The syllabus has two chapters: chapter 1 (introduction, rational use of medicines, evidence-based medicine, essential medicines and standard treatment guidelines) and chapter 2, which lists about 40 diseases in 13 body-system groups, (a) to (m). In this guide each group is a unit, except that:

- **infectious diseases (2g, 12 hours)** are split into two units (8 and 9), because they hold eight diseases;
- **musculoskeletal disorders and dermatology (2h and 2i, 3 hours each)** are joined in Unit 10;
- **ophthalmology and antimicrobial resistance (2k and 2l, 2 hours each)** are joined in Unit 12.

| Guide unit | Syllabus part | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Introduction, RUM, EBM, EML, STGs | Chapter 1 | 8 |
| 2. Cardiovascular: hypertension, angina, MI, hyperlipidaemia, CHF | 2(a) | 8 |
| 3. Respiratory: asthma, COPD | 2(b) | 4 |
| 4. Endocrine: diabetes, hypo- and hyperthyroidism | 2(c) | 5 |
| 5. CNS: epilepsy, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, stroke, migraine | 2(d) | 8 |
| 6. GI: GERD, peptic ulcer, alcoholic liver disease, IBD | 2(e) | 8 |
| 7. Haematological: iron deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia | 2(f) | 4 |
| 8. Infections I: TB, pneumonia, UTI, hepatitis | 2(g) | 12 (shared) |
| 9. Infections II: gonorrhoea, syphilis, malaria, HIV, SARS/COVID-19 | 2(g) | (shared) |
| 10. Rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, psoriasis, scabies, eczema | 2(h) + 2(i) | 3 + 3 |
| 11. Psychiatric: depression, anxiety, psychosis | 2(j) | 4 |
| 12. Conjunctivitis, glaucoma and antimicrobial resistance | 2(k) + 2(l) | 2 + 2 |
| 13. Women's health: PCOS, dysmenorrhoea, PMS | 2(m) | 4 |

## How to study a disease

The syllabus asks the same things for every disease: **definition, etiopathogenesis, clinical manifestations, non-pharmacological management and pharmacological management**. Learn every disease in that order, and add **counselling points**, because examiners and the practical (SOAP notes and counselling) both expect them. A good habit: after reading a disease, close the notes and write the five headings with three or four points under each.

Study one unit every two or three days. Draw each flow diagram (pathogenesis) once from memory, learn the comparison tables (asthma vs COPD, RA vs OA, UC vs Crohn's, hypo- vs hyperthyroidism, bacterial vs viral conjunctivitis), then answer the question bank without looking.

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 examinations are yearly and are conducted by the state examining body (in Himachal Pradesh, HPTSB) under the PCI ER-2020 regulations. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual ER-2020 paper looks like this; confirm the exact format with your college, because boards sometimes change it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide the **long** questions are 5-mark answers and the **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. A few **very-short** (2-mark) questions are included for quick revision and sessional tests.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years or a core topic with heavy syllabus weight; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for objective questions and as a backup choice.

Ratings are an estimate from the syllabus weight (hours) and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for Pharmacotherapeutics

1. **Use the five headings in every long answer:** definition → causes/risk factors → pathogenesis (a small flow diagram) → signs and symptoms → non-drug management → drug management (a table of drug groups with examples) → counselling. This structure alone earns most of the marks.
2. **Name drugs by group with two examples each** (for example "ACE inhibitors – enalapril, ramipril"). Generic names only.
3. **Mention the first-line drug** clearly: metformin in type 2 diabetes, ICS in asthma, SSRIs in depression, methotrexate in RA, permethrin in scabies, levodopa–carbidopa in Parkinson's, PPIs in GERD.
4. **Quote national programme regimens correctly:** TB 2HRZE/4HRE (NTEP), malaria – chloroquine + 14-day primaquine for vivax and ACT for falciparum, HIV – TLD.
5. **Give the key numbers:** BP 140/90; FPG 126, HbA1c 6.5%; Hb 13/12/11 g/dL; IOP 10–21 mmHg; CD4 below 200 for AIDS; FEV1/FVC below 0.70 in COPD; alteplase within 4.5 hours in stroke.
6. **Always finish with 3–4 counselling points** – they show pharmacist-level thinking and examiners reward them.
7. **Draw comparison tables** for "differentiate" questions; they are quicker to write and easier to mark.
8. **For a 3-mark short answer**, write 5–6 crisp points or a small table; do not write an essay.
9. Avoid writing doses unless you are sure; a wrong dose costs more than leaving it out.
10. The practical record (SOAP notes, counselling, dose calculations) uses the same knowledge – practise writing one SOAP note for each common disease.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, prepare full answers for: **rational use of medicines and essential medicines**, **hypertension**, **angina/MI**, **CHF**, **asthma vs COPD**, **diabetes**, **epilepsy**, **Parkinson's disease**, **peptic ulcer (H. pylori)**, **iron deficiency anaemia**, **tuberculosis**, **malaria**, **HIV**, **rheumatoid arthritis vs osteoarthritis**, **scabies**, **depression**, **glaucoma** and **antimicrobial resistance**.

## Chapter 1 basics

| Topic | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Rational use (WHO 1985) | Right drug, right dose, right duration, lowest cost |
| WHO good prescribing | 6 steps; P-drug = personal drug chosen in advance |
| EBM | Best evidence + clinical expertise + patient values; Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess |
| Strongest evidence | Systematic review / meta-analysis of RCTs |
| Essential medicines | WHO first list 1977; India NLEM first 1996, latest 2022 (384 medicines), generic names, P/S/T levels |
| STG | Preferred drug, dose, duration for a disease; supports RUM |
| SOAP | Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan |

## Diseases at a glance

| Disease | Key fact | First-line / key drugs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hypertension | 140/90 or more; 90–95% essential; silent | ACE inhibitor/ARB, CCB, thiazide; methyldopa/labetalol/nifedipine in pregnancy |
| Angina | Ischaemia without necrosis | SL nitroglycerin (attack); beta-blocker, CCB (variant), aspirin, statin |
| MI | Necrosis; troponin rise; ACS | Aspirin, second antiplatelet, reperfusion (PCI/thrombolysis), heparin; ABCDE |
| Hyperlipidaemia | LDL main target | Statins; fibrates for high TG; ezetimibe |
| CHF | ↓ pump; RAAS + sympathetic over-activity | ACEI/ARB/ARNI + beta-blocker + spironolactone + SGLT2 inhibitor; furosemide for oedema; daily weight |
| Asthma | Reversible, variable, inflammatory | ICS (cornerstone), ICS–formoterol reliever, SABA; never SABA or LABA alone |
| COPD | Not fully reversible; smoking, biomass; FEV1/FVC below 0.70 | LAMA/LABA; stop smoking; vaccines; O2 88–92% in exacerbation |
| Diabetes | FPG 126, OGTT 200, HbA1c 6.5% | Type 1 insulin; type 2 metformin + lifestyle; SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA for heart/kidney |
| Hypothyroidism | High TSH | Levothyroxine empty stomach, apart from iron/calcium |
| Hyperthyroidism | Low TSH; Graves' | Carbimazole (PTU early pregnancy), propranolol; sore throat → agranulocytosis |
| Epilepsy | Recurrent unprovoked seizures | Valproate (generalised), carbamazepine (focal), ethosuximide (absence); IV lorazepam in status |
| Parkinson's | Dopamine loss, TRAP | Levodopa + carbidopa; avoid metoclopramide |
| Alzheimer's | Plaques, tangles, ↓ ACh | Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine; memantine |
| Stroke | CT first; BE FAST | Alteplase within 4.5 h (ischaemic); aspirin, statin; anticoagulant in AF |
| Migraine | One-sided throbbing, photophobia | NSAIDs, triptans; propranolol, flunarizine prophylaxis |
| GERD | Weak LES; heartburn | PPI before breakfast + lifestyle |
| Peptic ulcer | *H. pylori*, NSAIDs | PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin 14 days; bismuth quadruple |
| Alcoholic liver disease | Fatty liver → hepatitis → cirrhosis | Abstinence, thiamine, benzodiazepines (withdrawal), spironolactone, lactulose, rifaximin |
| IBD | UC: colon, continuous; Crohn's: skip, transmural | Mesalamine, steroids for flares, azathioprine, anti-TNF |
| Iron deficiency anaemia | Microcytic; low ferritin, high TIBC | Ferrous sulfate; 3 months after Hb normal; black stools |
| Megaloblastic anaemia | Macrocytic; B12 → nerve damage | IM hydroxocobalamin; folic acid 5 mg; never folate alone in B12 lack |
| Tuberculosis | Cough 2 weeks+; CBNAAT | 2HRZE/4HRE; pyridoxine; rifampicin orange urine |
| Pneumonia | *S. pneumoniae*; CURB-65 | Amoxicillin / macrolide; ceftriaxone + azithromycin in hospital |
| UTI | *E. coli*; 10⁵ CFU/mL | Nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin; avoid fluoroquinolones in pregnancy |
| Hepatitis | A/E faeco-oral; B/C blood | B – tenofovir/entecavir, vaccine; C – sofosbuvir-based DAAs 12 weeks |
| Gonorrhoea | Gram-negative diplococci | Ceftriaxone + azithromycin; treat partner |
| Syphilis | Painless chancre; VDRL/TPHA | Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM |
| Malaria | *Anopheles*; vivax relapses | Vivax: chloroquine + primaquine 14 days; falciparum: ACT + single primaquine; severe: IV artesunate |
| HIV | CD4 below 200 = AIDS | Treat all; TLD; PEP within 72 h for 28 days; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis |
| COVID-19 | SARS-CoV-2, ACE2 | Mild – home care; oxygen-requiring – dexamethasone + anticoagulant; vaccines |
| Rheumatoid arthritis | Symmetrical small joints; stiffness more than 1 h | Methotrexate weekly + folic acid; biologics |
| Osteoarthritis | Weight-bearing joints; pain on use | Weight loss, exercise, topical NSAID, paracetamol |
| Psoriasis | Silvery plaques, Auspitz sign | Topical steroid + calcipotriol; methotrexate; no systemic steroids |
| Scabies | Night itch, burrows | Permethrin 5% neck down 8–12 h, repeat day 7; treat contacts |
| Eczema | Barrier defect, itch | Emollients daily + topical steroid; tacrolimus |
| Depression | 2 weeks, SIG E CAPS | SSRIs; 2–4 weeks to act; continue 6–12 months; taper |
| Anxiety | Excess worry, panic | CBT + SSRI/SNRI; benzodiazepines 2–4 weeks only |
| Psychosis | Hallucinations, delusions; dopamine excess | Antipsychotics; EPS (typical), weight gain (atypical), clozapine needs blood counts |
| Conjunctivitis | Bacterial purulent; viral watery | Topical antibiotic for bacterial only; hygiene |
| Glaucoma | Optic nerve damage; IOP 10–21 normal | Latanoprost, timolol, brimonidine, dorzolamide; acute: acetazolamide, mannitol, pilocarpine |
| AMR | Enzymes, target change, efflux, low permeability | Stewardship; Schedule H1 2013, Red Line 2016, NAP-AMR 2017 |
| PCOS | Rotterdam 2 of 3 | Weight loss; COC; metformin; letrozole/clomiphene |
| Dysmenorrhoea | Prostaglandins | NSAIDs early + heat; COC |
| PMS | Luteal phase symptoms | Lifestyle, calcium; SSRIs; drospirenone COC |

## Danger signs to quote in counselling answers

- Chest pain not relieved by nitrate in 5 minutes → emergency.
- Weight gain of about 2 kg in 2–3 days in heart failure → call the doctor.
- Sore throat and fever on carbimazole or clozapine → blood count.
- Rash on carbamazepine or lamotrigine → stop and report.
- Yellow eyes on TB drugs → liver check; blurred colour vision on ethambutol.
- Dark urine on primaquine → stop, check G6PD.
- Painful red eye with reduced vision or haloes → urgent eye referral.
- Thoughts of self-harm on antidepressants → seek help at once.

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of hypertension

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) note for a clinical case of essential hypertension and to identify drug-related problems and counselling needs.

## Principle

A SOAP note is a structured record of a patient's problem. **Subjective** data are what the patient reports, **objective** data are measured findings, the **assessment** is the pharmacist's judgement of the problem and the therapy, and the **plan** lists drug and non-drug measures, monitoring and counselling. In hypertension the aim is to reach the target BP (commonly below 140/90 mmHg, lower in diabetes or kidney disease if tolerated), protect target organs and improve adherence.

## Requirements

Case sheet or hypothetical case, prescription, laboratory reports, BP apparatus (sphygmomanometer and stethoscope or digital monitor), weighing scale, measuring tape, references (National Formulary of India, standard treatment guidelines), SOAP format sheet.

## Procedure

1. Read the case and list the patient's details (age, sex, occupation, weight, height).
2. Record the **subjective** data: chief complaints, duration, past history, medication history, allergies, diet (salt), smoking, alcohol, exercise, family history.
3. Record the **objective** data: BP (two readings, seated, after 5 minutes' rest), pulse, BMI, waist, laboratory values (creatinine, potassium, sugar, lipids, urine protein), ECG.
4. Classify the BP and identify risk factors and target-organ damage.
5. Review each prescribed drug for indication, dose, interactions, contraindications and adverse effects; list drug-related problems (DRPs).
6. Write the **assessment**: diagnosis, control status and DRPs.
7. Write the **plan**: drug therapy changes (as suggested to the prescriber), non-drug measures, monitoring parameters and follow-up, and counselling points.
8. Discuss the case with the teacher and record corrections.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr R, 52 years, clerk, comes for refill. Diagnosed with hypertension 1 year ago, on enalapril. Complains of a dry irritating cough for 2 months and occasional morning headache. Smokes 10 cigarettes a day; eats pickles daily; no exercise. Father had a stroke.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Dry cough 2 months, morning headache; smoker; high salt intake; sedentary; family history of stroke; takes medicine "only when headache comes" |
| **O** | BP 158/98 and 154/96 mmHg; pulse 82/min; weight 84 kg, height 1.70 m, BMI about 29 kg/m²; serum creatinine and potassium normal; fasting glucose 98 mg/dL; LDL 150 mg/dL |
| **A** | Stage 1 essential hypertension, **uncontrolled**. DRPs: (1) adverse drug reaction – dry cough due to the ACE inhibitor; (2) **non-adherence** (takes drug only when symptomatic); (3) untreated risk factors – smoking, obesity, salt, raised LDL |
| **P** | Suggest to prescriber: change enalapril to an **ARB** (e.g. losartan or telmisartan) – no cough; add amlodipine if BP stays above target. Consider a statin after cardiovascular risk assessment. Non-drug: salt below about 5 g/day, avoid pickles, brisk walk 30 min on most days, weight loss, stop smoking (refer to cessation support). Monitor: home BP log, review in 2–4 weeks, creatinine and potassium after starting/changing ARB. Counsel as below |

**Counselling points given:** hypertension is usually silent – take tablets daily even without headache; same time each day; do not double a missed dose; rise slowly; report dizziness, swelling of lips or face; avoid pain-killers (NSAIDs) and decongestants without advice; keep a BP diary.

## Result

A SOAP note for a case of uncontrolled essential hypertension was prepared; ACE-inhibitor cough and non-adherence were identified as drug-related problems, and a therapy plan and counselling were proposed.

## Precautions

1. Measure BP correctly – correct cuff size, arm at heart level, patient seated and rested, no smoking or caffeine 30 minutes before.
2. Keep patient information confidential.
3. Recommendations are made to the prescriber; the pharmacist does not change therapy alone.
4. Use generic names and current guidelines.

## Viva questions

1. **What does SOAP stand for?** Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan.
2. **Which antihypertensive causes dry cough?** ACE inhibitors (enalapril, ramipril) – due to bradykinin.
3. **Why switch to an ARB?** ARBs give the same benefit without cough.
4. **Target BP for most adults?** Below 140/90 mmHg; often below 130/80 in diabetes or kidney disease if tolerated.
5. **Name two first-line drug groups.** ACE inhibitors/ARBs, CCBs, thiazides (any two).
6. **Salt advice?** Less than about 5 g salt per day.
practicals.title: SOAP note: hypertension

# SOAP note for a clinical case of angina pectoris

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of stable angina pectoris.

## Principle

Stable angina is chest pain due to temporary myocardial ischaemia on exertion. Therapy aims to relieve attacks (sublingual nitrate), prevent attacks (beta-blocker or CCB, long-acting nitrate) and prevent MI and death (aspirin, statin, risk-factor control). The SOAP note helps check that all three aims are covered and that the patient can use the nitrate correctly.

## Requirements

Case sheet, prescription, ECG and lipid reports, BP apparatus, references (NFI, standard treatment guidelines), demonstration sublingual tablet bottle or spray, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Note patient details and the nature of chest pain (site, radiation, duration, trigger, relief).
2. Record risk factors: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, lipids, family history, obesity.
3. Record vital signs, ECG (rest/stress), lipid profile, sugar.
4. Check whether the prescription has (a) a reliever, (b) an anti-anginal preventer, (c) aspirin and a statin.
5. Look for interactions (nitrate with sildenafil) and contraindications (beta-blocker in asthma).
6. Write assessment, plan and counselling; discuss with the teacher.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mrs S, 60 years, diabetic, gets chest tightness on climbing stairs that goes after 3–4 minutes' rest. Prescribed isosorbide mononitrate and sublingual nitroglycerin. She sometimes swallows the sublingual tablet. She keeps the tablets in a pill box in her purse.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Exertional chest tightness for 3 months, relieved by rest; type 2 diabetes for 8 years on metformin; non-smoker; tablets kept in a pill box |
| **O** | BP 146/90 mmHg; pulse 88/min; ECG: ST depression on stress test; LDL 132 mg/dL; HbA1c 7.8% |
| **A** | Stable angina; BP and diabetes not at target. DRPs: (1) **no antiplatelet and no statin** (indication without drug); (2) **wrong technique** – swallowing the SL tablet; (3) **improper storage** of nitroglycerin; (4) no beta-blocker for symptom prevention |
| **P** | Suggest: low-dose aspirin, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker (e.g. metoprolol) to prevent attacks and lower heart rate; ACE inhibitor for diabetes with high BP. Keep the nitrate-free interval for isosorbide mononitrate. Non-drug: graded walking, diet, weight control. Monitor: frequency of attacks, pulse, BP, lipids, HbA1c |

**Counselling:** at onset of pain sit down and put one tablet **under the tongue** (do not swallow); if not better in 5 minutes take another and call an ambulance; headache is common; keep tablets in the **original airtight glass bottle**, away from heat and light; never with sildenafil-type drugs; report pain at rest or more frequent attacks.

## Result

The SOAP note identified missing preventive therapy and incorrect nitrate use and storage, and a plan with counselling was prepared.

## Precautions

1. Unstable or rest pain must be referred urgently.
2. Check BP and pulse before advising beta-blockers.
3. Recommendations go to the prescriber.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the SL nitrate placed under the tongue?** Rapid absorption, bypasses first-pass metabolism.
2. **What is nitrate tolerance?** Loss of effect with continuous use; prevented by a nitrate-free interval.
3. **Drug of choice in variant angina?** Calcium channel blocker.
4. **Why add aspirin and a statin?** To prevent MI and death.
5. **Main interaction of nitrates?** PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) – severe hypotension.
practicals.title: SOAP note: angina pectoris

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of myocardial infarction

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a patient recovering from acute myocardial infarction, with emphasis on secondary prevention and discharge counselling.

## Principle

After MI, long-term drugs reduce re-infarction and death: antiplatelets, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/ARB, high-intensity statin (and aldosterone antagonist if heart function is low), with life-style change and cardiac rehabilitation ("ABCDE"). The pharmacist checks that each is present, at a suitable dose, and that the patient understands why.

## Requirements

Discharge summary or hypothetical case, ECG, troponin, echocardiography and lipid reports, prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Summarise the event: date, type (STEMI/NSTEMI), reperfusion done (PCI/thrombolysis), complications.
2. Record history: risk factors, other diseases, allergies, current drugs.
3. Record vital signs, ejection fraction, creatinine, potassium, lipids, sugar.
4. Check the discharge prescription against the ABCDE list.
5. Look for interactions (e.g. clopidogrel with omeprazole, NSAIDs with antiplatelets).
6. Write assessment, plan, monitoring and discharge counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr K, 48 years, smoker, admitted with anterior STEMI; primary PCI with stent done. Discharge drugs: aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, ramipril, atorvastatin (high intensity), sublingual nitrate. He asks whether he can stop "blood thinners" after a month, and takes diclofenac for back pain.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Chest pain 5 days ago; smoker 20/day; back pain treated with diclofenac; wants to stop antiplatelets early |
| **O** | BP 124/78 mmHg; pulse 66/min; troponin was raised; EF 40%; LDL 168 mg/dL; creatinine and potassium normal |
| **A** | Post-STEMI with stent, reduced EF. Prescription covers ABCDE. DRPs: (1) **risk of premature stopping of dual antiplatelets** (stent thrombosis); (2) **NSAID use** with antiplatelets (bleeding, CV risk); (3) continued smoking |
| **P** | Continue aspirin + ticagrelor for the period advised (often 12 months), then aspirin long term; continue metoprolol, ramipril, atorvastatin; consider aldosterone antagonist for low EF (prescriber). Replace diclofenac with paracetamol. Smoking cessation support. Cardiac rehabilitation referral. Monitor BP, pulse, lipids at 6–8 weeks, liver enzymes, potassium and creatinine |

**Counselling:** never stop antiplatelets without the cardiologist's advice; report black stools, blood in urine or unusual bruising; carry SL nitrate – if chest pain is not relieved after one dose in 5 minutes call emergency; stop smoking completely; walk daily as advised; heart-healthy diet; avoid over-the-counter pain-killers like diclofenac and ibuprofen.

## Result

A post-MI SOAP note was prepared; NSAID use and the risk of stopping dual antiplatelet therapy were identified and corrected, and discharge counselling was planned.

## Precautions

1. Avoid NSAIDs in post-MI patients.
2. Check heart rate and BP before beta-blocker titration.
3. Maintain confidentiality; advice to prescriber only.

## Viva questions

1. **Marker for MI?** Cardiac troponin.
2. **Expand ABCDE.** Aspirin/ACE inhibitor, Beta-blocker/BP, Cholesterol/Cigarettes, Diet/Diabetes, Exercise/Education.
3. **Why is DAPT important after stent?** Prevents stent thrombosis.
4. **Name two thrombolytics.** Streptokinase, tenecteplase (or alteplase).
5. **Most common cause of early death after MI?** Arrhythmias.
practicals.title: SOAP note: myocardial infarction

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of hyperlipidaemia

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of hyperlipidaemia (dyslipidaemia).

## Principle

Raised LDL-cholesterol causes atherosclerosis. Management is based on the patient's overall cardiovascular risk: life-style change for all and a statin for those at higher risk or with very high LDL; fibrates for very high triglycerides. Secondary causes (hypothyroidism, diabetes, drugs) must be found and treated.

## Requirements

Case details, fasting lipid profile, sugar, TSH, liver function, prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record history: diet, alcohol, exercise, smoking, family history of early heart disease, other diseases and drugs.
2. Record BMI, waist, BP and the lipid profile; calculate non-HDL cholesterol (total – HDL).
3. Look for secondary causes.
4. Assess cardiovascular risk and decide the goal.
5. Review the prescribed lipid-lowering drug for suitability, interactions and adverse effects.
6. Write the assessment, plan and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr D, 45 years, office worker, BMI 28. Fasting lipids: total cholesterol 262, LDL 178, HDL 36, triglycerides 240 mg/dL. Complains of tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold. Prescribed atorvastatin. Drinks alcohol at weekends.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Tiredness, cold intolerance, weight gain; weekend alcohol; fried food, no exercise |
| **O** | BMI 28; BP 132/84; lipids as above; non-HDL 226 mg/dL; TSH 12 mIU/L (high) |
| **A** | Mixed dyslipidaemia. DRP: **secondary cause not treated** – hypothyroidism (raises LDL and increases statin muscle-toxicity risk) |
| **P** | Suggest levothyroxine for hypothyroidism and recheck lipids after the thyroid is normal; continue statin as per risk assessment. Non-drug: less saturated fat, no trans fat, more fibre, reduce alcohol (triglycerides), 150 minutes of exercise per week, weight loss. Monitor: lipids 6–8 weeks after changes, liver enzymes if symptoms, muscle symptoms |

**Counselling:** take the statin regularly (atorvastatin any time of day); report unexplained muscle pain, weakness or dark urine; continue diet and exercise – drugs are not a replacement; limit alcohol; regular lipid checks.

## Result

A SOAP note for mixed dyslipidaemia was prepared; untreated hypothyroidism was identified as a secondary cause, and a combined drug and life-style plan was suggested.

## Precautions

Fasting sample for triglycerides; statins avoided in pregnancy; check interactions (gemfibrozil, some macrolides, azole antifungals raise statin levels).

## Viva questions

1. **Main lipid target?** LDL-cholesterol.
2. **Low HDL level?** Below 40 mg/dL.
3. **Serious adverse effect of statins?** Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis.
4. **Drug for very high triglycerides?** Fenofibrate (and omega-3 fatty acids).
5. **Two secondary causes?** Hypothyroidism, diabetes (also nephrotic syndrome, alcohol, thiazides).
practicals.title: SOAP note: hyperlipidaemia

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of rheumatoid arthritis

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of rheumatoid arthritis, with emphasis on safe methotrexate therapy.

## Principle

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune polyarthritis. Early DMARD therapy (methotrexate as the anchor drug) prevents joint damage; NSAIDs and short courses of steroids only relieve symptoms. Methotrexate is given **once weekly** with folic acid and needs blood monitoring – dosing errors and missed monitoring are common drug-related problems.

## Requirements

Case sheet, prescription, CBC, liver and kidney function tests, ESR/CRP, RF and anti-CCP reports, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record joint symptoms (which joints, symmetry, morning stiffness duration), function, fatigue.
2. Record other diseases, pregnancy plans, alcohol, infections (TB, hepatitis B history).
3. Record joint count, ESR/CRP, blood counts, liver and kidney tests.
4. Check DMARD schedule, folic acid, NSAID use with gastroprotection, steroid dose.
5. Identify DRPs, write the plan and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mrs P, 38 years, school teacher, painful swollen fingers and wrists on both sides for 5 months with morning stiffness of 2 hours. Started on methotrexate; the strip label reads "once a week" but she has been taking one tablet every day for 6 days and now has mouth ulcers. She also takes diclofenac twice daily on an empty stomach.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Symmetrical small-joint pain, morning stiffness 2 hours, fatigue; mouth ulcers for 2 days; diclofenac twice daily without food; plans pregnancy next year |
| **O** | Tender, swollen MCP and PIP joints both hands; ESR 52 mm/h; CRP raised; RF and anti-CCP positive; WBC mildly low; liver enzymes mildly raised |
| **A** | Active RA. DRPs: (1) **methotrexate taken daily instead of weekly** – toxicity (mouth ulcers, low WBC, raised enzymes) – urgent; (2) NSAID without gastroprotection or food; (3) no folic acid; (4) pregnancy plan while on a teratogenic drug |
| **P** | Contact prescriber at once: stop methotrexate, assess toxicity (folinic acid rescue as decided by the doctor), repeat CBC and LFT. Restart weekly dosing when safe, with folic acid on another day. Take NSAID with food; add PPI if needed. Reliable contraception; plan pregnancy with the rheumatologist (methotrexate must be stopped months before). Physiotherapy and exercise |

**Counselling:** methotrexate is taken **only once a week on the same day** (mark it on a calendar); folic acid on a different day; regular blood tests; avoid alcohol; report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, breathlessness or bruising; avoid cotrimoxazole and extra pain-killers without advice; use contraception.

## Result

A serious medication error (daily methotrexate) and other DRPs were identified in an RA patient; an urgent plan and detailed counselling were prepared.

## Precautions

Methotrexate dosing errors are life-threatening – always confirm the weekly day; screen for TB and hepatitis B before biologics; no live vaccines on immunosuppressants.

## Viva questions

1. **Anchor DMARD in RA?** Methotrexate.
2. **Why folic acid with methotrexate?** Reduces side effects such as mouth ulcers and nausea.
3. **Antibodies seen in RA?** Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP.
4. **Which joints are spared in RA?** Distal interphalangeal joints.
5. **Eye check is needed for which DMARD?** Hydroxychloroquine.
practicals.title: SOAP note: rheumatoid arthritis

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of asthma

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of bronchial asthma and to check inhaler technique.

## Principle

Asthma control depends on regular inhaled corticosteroid, correct inhaler technique, trigger avoidance and adherence. Over-use of the reliever (salbutamol) is a sign of poor control. The SOAP note documents control, finds the cause of poor control and plans treatment changes and counselling.

## Requirements

Case details, prescription, placebo metered-dose inhaler and spacer, peak flow meter, spirometry report, references (GINA summary, STG), SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record symptoms: daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use per week, activity limitation, attacks in the last year.
2. Record triggers, smoking or smoke exposure, other diseases (rhinitis, GERD), drugs (beta-blockers, NSAIDs).
3. Record PEF or FEV1, oxygen saturation, eosinophils.
4. **Ask the patient to demonstrate the inhaler** and note errors.
5. Assess control (well, partly, poorly controlled) and identify DRPs.
6. Write the plan: step up/down, technique correction, action plan, counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Rahul, 19 years, college student, uses a salbutamol inhaler 5–6 times a week and wakes at night with cough twice a week. Prescribed a budesonide inhaler 3 months ago but "uses it only when breathless". Lives near a construction site. Demonstration: does not shake the inhaler, breathes in fast, no breath-hold.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Daytime symptoms more than twice a week, night waking, reliever use 5–6 times/week, ICS used only when breathless; dust exposure |
| **O** | PEF 70% of personal best; SpO2 97%; poor MDI technique observed |
| **A** | **Poorly controlled asthma**. DRPs: (1) **non-adherence to ICS** (controller used as reliever); (2) **poor inhaler technique**; (3) SABA over-use; (4) trigger exposure |
| **P** | Correct technique and add a spacer; daily ICS (or switch to ICS–formoterol as maintenance and reliever, as decided by the prescriber); review in 4–6 weeks before stepping up further; written asthma action plan; mask in dusty areas; influenza vaccine. Monitor reliever use, night symptoms, PEF diary |

**Counselling:** explain reliever versus preventer; preventer every day even when well; shake, breathe out, slow deep breath while pressing, hold 10 seconds; rinse mouth after ICS; seek care if reliever needed more often or not working.

## Result

Poor asthma control due to ICS non-adherence and wrong technique was identified; technique was corrected and a plan with an action plan was prepared.

## Precautions

Use placebo inhalers for demonstration; refer urgently if signs of a severe attack (cannot speak, cyanosis, silent chest).

## Viva questions

1. **Sign of poor asthma control?** Reliever use more than twice a week, night waking, activity limitation.
2. **Why rinse after ICS?** Prevent oral thrush.
3. **Breath-hold after MDI?** About 10 seconds.
4. **Why should LABA not be used alone in asthma?** Increases risk of severe attacks without treating inflammation.
5. **Use of a spacer?** Removes need for coordination; more drug to lungs, less in mouth.
practicals.title: SOAP note: asthma

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of COPD

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

## Principle

COPD causes persistent, progressive airflow limitation, mainly from smoking and biomass smoke. Management: stop exposure, long-acting bronchodilators (LAMA/LABA), vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation, and early treatment of exacerbations. Inhaler handling (especially capsule devices) is a frequent problem.

## Requirements

Case details, spirometry report, prescription, placebo dry powder (capsule) inhaler, pulse oximeter, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record breathlessness (mMRC grade), cough, sputum, exacerbations in the past year, hospital admissions.
2. Record smoking (pack-years) and biomass exposure, other diseases (heart failure, diabetes).
3. Record spirometry (FEV1/FVC, FEV1 % predicted), SpO2, BMI.
4. Check inhaler device and technique; vaccination status.
5. Identify DRPs; write plan and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr H, 66 years, farmer, smoker of beedis for 40 years. Breathless on walking 100 m; morning cough with sputum. Prescribed tiotropium capsules for inhalation; he has been **swallowing the capsules**. Two exacerbations in the past year. Never vaccinated.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Progressive breathlessness, chronic productive cough, continuing smoker, swallowing inhalation capsules, two exacerbations/year |
| **O** | Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58, FEV1 48% predicted; SpO2 93% at rest; BMI 19 |
| **A** | COPD, moderate–severe airflow limitation, frequent exacerbations. DRPs: (1) **wrong route** – inhalation capsule swallowed; (2) continued smoking; (3) no vaccination |
| **P** | Teach capsule inhaler use (load, pierce, breathe in deeply, hold breath); consider LAMA + LABA combination (prescriber); smoking cessation counselling with nicotine replacement; influenza and pneumococcal vaccines; pulmonary rehabilitation; nutrition support; written plan for early signs of exacerbation. Monitor symptoms, exacerbations, SpO2 |

**Counselling:** the capsule must be placed in the device and inhaled, never swallowed; stop smoking – the most important step; avoid smoke from fires; pursed-lip breathing; seek care early if sputum turns yellow-green or breathlessness worsens.

## Result

A COPD SOAP note was prepared; incorrect administration (swallowing inhalation capsules), smoking and missing vaccination were identified and addressed.

## Precautions

Use controlled oxygen in COPD; check for heart failure; demonstration devices only.

## Viva questions

1. **Spirometric criterion for COPD?** Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.
2. **Most effective intervention?** Smoking cessation.
3. **Example of LAMA?** Tiotropium.
4. **Why are ICS used carefully in COPD?** Raise pneumonia risk; reserved for frequent exacerbators.
5. **Vaccines recommended?** Influenza (yearly) and pneumococcal.
practicals.title: SOAP note: COPD

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of diabetes mellitus

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

## Principle

Type 2 diabetes is managed by life-style change, metformin first, and other drugs chosen by the patient's needs (heart or kidney disease, weight, cost, hypoglycaemia risk). Targets usually include HbA1c below 7%, BP and lipid control, and prevention of complications. Hypoglycaemia and poor foot care are common preventable problems.

## Requirements

Case details, prescription, glucometer, HbA1c, lipid, creatinine/eGFR, urine albumin reports, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record symptoms, duration of diabetes, diet, activity, hypoglycaemic episodes, complications (eyes, feet, kidneys, heart).
2. Record weight, BMI, BP, FPG, PPG, HbA1c, lipids, kidney function, urine albumin.
3. Review each antidiabetic drug: timing in relation to meals, dose for kidney function, hypoglycaemia risk.
4. Identify DRPs; write plan, monitoring and counselling (diet, foot care, hypoglycaemia).

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mrs N, 55 years, type 2 diabetes for 6 years, on metformin and glimepiride. Skips lunch on fasting days and has had sweating and shaking twice. Walks barefoot at home; has a small painless crack on the heel. Also has hypertension (not on treatment).

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Two episodes of sweating/tremor on fasting days; barefoot at home; painless heel crack; tingling feet |
| **O** | BMI 30; BP 148/92 mmHg; FPG 168 mg/dL; HbA1c 8.4%; eGFR normal; urine albumin raised; reduced foot sensation on monofilament test |
| **A** | Uncontrolled type 2 diabetes with neuropathy and early nephropathy; hypertension untreated. DRPs: (1) **hypoglycaemia** from sulfonylurea with skipped meals; (2) **untreated indication** – hypertension with albuminuria (needs ACEI/ARB); (3) foot-care risk |
| **P** | Suggest: replace glimepiride with a drug of low hypoglycaemia risk (DPP-4 inhibitor or SGLT2 inhibitor – kidney benefit) per prescriber; add ACE inhibitor/ARB; statin per risk. Diet plan with regular meals; walk 30 minutes daily. Foot care education and referral for the heel crack. Monitor: home glucose, HbA1c after 3 months, BP, kidney function and potassium |

**Counselling:** recognise hypoglycaemia and treat with 15 g sugar, recheck in 15 minutes; never skip meals on these drugs; take metformin with food; inspect feet daily, never walk barefoot, moisturise but not between toes, see a doctor for any wound; yearly eye and kidney check.

## Result

A SOAP note for uncontrolled type 2 diabetes was prepared; drug-induced hypoglycaemia, untreated hypertension with albuminuria and foot risk were identified and addressed.

## Precautions

Adjust metformin and other drugs for kidney function; check glucometer technique; confidentiality.

## Viva questions

1. **HbA1c target for most adults?** Below 7%.
2. **Drug class most likely to cause hypoglycaemia (oral)?** Sulfonylureas.
3. **Rule of 15?** 15 g fast sugar, recheck after 15 minutes.
4. **Antihypertensive preferred in diabetes with albuminuria?** ACE inhibitor or ARB.
5. **Adverse effect of long-term metformin?** Vitamin B12 deficiency.
practicals.title: SOAP note: diabetes mellitus

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of epilepsy

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of epilepsy.

## Principle

Seizure control depends on the right antiepileptic for the seizure type, regular adherence, avoidance of triggers and attention to interactions and special groups (women who may become pregnant). Breakthrough seizures are most often due to missed doses, sleep loss, alcohol or interacting drugs.

## Requirements

Case details, seizure diary, EEG/MRI report, drug levels (if available), prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record seizure type, frequency, last seizure, triggers, adherence, other drugs (including contraceptives), pregnancy plans.
2. Record examination, EEG/imaging, sodium, liver tests, drug level.
3. Check suitability of the drug for seizure type and patient (age, sex), dose and interactions.
4. Identify DRPs, write plan, safety advice and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Ms A, 24 years, generalised tonic–clonic seizures, seizure-free for one year on sodium valproate. Recently married, planning pregnancy; started a combined oral contraceptive. Had one seizure last week after night duty and missing two doses.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Breakthrough seizure after sleep loss and two missed doses; wants pregnancy soon; on combined pill |
| **O** | Neurological exam normal; EEG generalised discharges; liver tests normal; weight gain 6 kg in a year |
| **A** | Generalised epilepsy with breakthrough seizure. DRPs: (1) **non-adherence and sleep deprivation**; (2) **valproate in a woman planning pregnancy** – high teratogenic risk; (3) no folic acid |
| **P** | Refer to neurologist for a planned switch to a safer drug (e.g. levetiracetam or lamotrigine) **before** conception, done gradually; start folic acid; note: lamotrigine levels fall with oestrogen-containing pills (dose review if switched). Sleep hygiene, avoid alcohol; pill box and phone reminders. Monitor seizure diary |

**Counselling:** never stop or change the drug suddenly; take at fixed times; if a dose is missed take it when remembered unless near the next dose; regular sleep; avoid alcohol; no driving, swimming alone or working at heights until seizure-free as advised; inform the doctor before pregnancy; family first aid (recovery position, nothing in mouth, call help if longer than 5 minutes).

## Result

A SOAP note for generalised epilepsy was prepared; non-adherence, sleep loss and valproate use in a woman planning pregnancy were identified, and a safe plan was suggested.

## Precautions

Never stop antiepileptics abruptly; check interactions with enzyme inducers; switching drugs only under specialist care.

## Viva questions

1. **Drug of choice for absence seizures?** Ethosuximide (or valproate).
2. **Why avoid valproate in pregnancy?** Neural tube defects and developmental problems.
3. **First drug in status epilepticus?** IV lorazepam or diazepam.
4. **Two adverse effects of phenytoin?** Gum hypertrophy, hirsutism (also ataxia).
5. **Which antiepileptic reduces the effect of oral contraceptives?** Carbamazepine (also phenytoin, phenobarbitone).
practicals.title: SOAP note: epilepsy

practicals.markdown:
# SOAP note for a clinical case of stroke

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a patient after an ischaemic stroke, focusing on secondary prevention.

## Principle

After ischaemic stroke the risk of another stroke is high. Secondary prevention includes an antiplatelet (or an anticoagulant if atrial fibrillation), a statin, BP and diabetes control, smoking cessation and rehabilitation. Haemorrhagic stroke must be excluded by CT before any antithrombotic.

## Requirements

Case details, CT/MRI report, ECG (atrial fibrillation), lipid profile, sugar, prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record onset, type of stroke, deficits (weakness, speech, swallowing), treatment given (thrombolysis).
2. Record risk factors: BP, diabetes, AF, smoking, lipids, previous TIA.
3. Record BP, ECG, lipids, HbA1c, swallowing assessment.
4. Check the prescription: antithrombotic choice, statin, antihypertensive, dosage form suitable for swallowing.
5. Identify DRPs, plan and counselling for patient and caregiver.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr V, 68 years, ischaemic stroke with right-sided weakness; CT showed infarct, no bleed. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Discharge prescription: aspirin, atorvastatin, amlodipine. He has difficulty swallowing large tablets.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Weakness right side, slurred speech improving; difficulty swallowing tablets; caregiver is his daughter |
| **O** | BP 150/92 mmHg; pulse irregular; ECG atrial fibrillation; LDL 142 mg/dL; HbA1c 6.1% |
| **A** | Ischaemic stroke with atrial fibrillation. DRPs: (1) **anticoagulant indicated but not prescribed** – aspirin alone is inadequate for AF-related stroke prevention; (2) BP above target; (3) dosage-form problem (dysphagia) |
| **P** | Suggest oral anticoagulant (apixaban, dabigatran or warfarin, timing as decided by the neurologist) in place of aspirin; continue statin; optimise BP; dosage forms suitable for swallowing difficulty (crushable tablets or liquids where appropriate – not for modified-release forms); physiotherapy and speech therapy. Monitor BP, bleeding, INR if warfarin, kidney function |

**Counselling (patient and caregiver):** take the blood thinner exactly as advised; report black stools, blood in urine, gum bleeding or severe headache; with warfarin keep INR appointments and a consistent diet, check before new medicines; BE FAST warning signs – go to hospital immediately; control BP, stop smoking.

## Result

A post-stroke SOAP note was prepared; missing anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, uncontrolled BP and a dosage-form problem were identified and a plan was proposed.

## Precautions

No antithrombotic before CT excludes bleeding; check whether a tablet can be crushed; caregiver education is essential.

## Viva questions

1. **First investigation in suspected stroke?** CT scan of the brain.
2. **Thrombolytic in ischaemic stroke and time window?** Alteplase within about 4.5 hours.
3. **Most important risk factor?** Hypertension.
4. **Why anticoagulant in AF?** AF causes clots in the heart that embolise to the brain.
5. **Expand BE FAST.** Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time.
practicals.title: SOAP note: stroke

# SOAP note for a clinical case of depression

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of depression.

## Principle

Depression is treated with psychotherapy and antidepressants (SSRIs first line). Early drop-out is common because benefit takes 2–4 weeks while side effects come first. Assessment must include suicide risk, and counselling must be supportive and non-judgemental.

## Requirements

Case details, PHQ-9 or similar scale, thyroid test, prescription, references, SOAP sheet, a quiet private place for discussion.

## Procedure

1. Record mood symptoms (SIG E CAPS), duration, stressors, sleep, appetite, alcohol, previous episodes, family history.
2. **Ask directly about suicidal thoughts**; note risk.
3. Record PHQ-9 score, weight, TSH, other illnesses and drugs that can cause depression.
4. Review the antidepressant: dose, duration so far, side effects, interactions.
5. Identify DRPs; write plan and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Ms M, 29 years, software engineer, low mood, loss of interest, poor sleep and appetite for 6 weeks after a job loss. Started sertraline 10 days ago; stopped it because "it is not working and gives nausea". No suicidal plan but feels hopeless at times. Takes tramadol occasionally for headache.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, poor appetite, hopelessness; stopped sertraline after 10 days due to nausea and "no effect"; occasional tramadol |
| **O** | PHQ-9 score 17 (moderately severe); weight loss 3 kg; TSH normal |
| **A** | Moderate–severe depression. DRPs: (1) **non-adherence** due to unrealistic expectation of quick effect and early side effects; (2) **interaction risk** – tramadol with SSRI (serotonin syndrome, seizures); (3) suicide risk needs monitoring |
| **P** | Restart sertraline after taking it with food (nausea settles in 1–2 weeks) – confirm with prescriber; refer for CBT; avoid tramadol – use paracetamol for headache; follow-up in 1–2 weeks, then regularly; give crisis contact numbers. Monitor PHQ-9, side effects, suicidal thoughts |

**Counselling:** medicine is not habit-forming; benefit begins in 2–4 weeks; nausea usually settles; take after breakfast; continue for months after recovery; never stop suddenly; avoid alcohol and tramadol; contact the doctor or a helpline immediately if thoughts of self-harm increase; regular exercise, routine and support from family or friends.

## Result

A SOAP note for depression was prepared; premature stopping of the SSRI and a tramadol interaction were identified, and supportive counselling with a monitoring plan was provided.

## Precautions

Assess suicide risk sensitively; maintain strict confidentiality; dispense limited quantities if risk is high; refer urgently if active suicidal intent.

## Viva questions

1. **First-line antidepressants?** SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram).
2. **When does the effect start?** About 2–4 weeks.
3. **How long to continue after remission?** At least 6–12 months.
4. **What is discontinuation syndrome?** Dizziness, irritability, flu-like symptoms on stopping suddenly.
5. **Drugs causing serotonin syndrome with SSRIs?** MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, triptans.
practicals.title: SOAP note: depression

# SOAP note for a clinical case of tuberculosis

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of pulmonary tuberculosis treated under the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP).

## Principle

Drug-sensitive TB is treated with daily weight-band fixed-dose combinations: 2HRZE in the intensive phase and 4HRE in the continuation phase. Success depends on adherence, monitoring for hepatotoxicity and other adverse effects, nutrition, and testing for HIV and diabetes. Rifampicin interacts with many drugs.

## Requirements

Case details, sputum/CBNAAT report, chest X-ray, LFT, HIV and blood sugar results, weight, NTEP treatment card, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record symptoms (cough, fever, weight loss), contact history, previous TB treatment, other diseases and drugs.
2. Record weight (for weight band), sputum/CBNAAT result (rifampicin sensitivity), X-ray, LFT, HIV, sugar.
3. Check regimen, weight-band dose and phase; check interactions (oral contraceptives, antiretrovirals, warfarin).
4. Identify DRPs and adverse effects; write plan, monitoring and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr J, 34 years, labourer, 46 kg. New sputum-positive pulmonary TB, rifampicin-sensitive. In the 6th week of treatment he complains of tingling in the feet and has stopped tablets for 4 days because "the urine is red". Drinks alcohol daily. Blood sugar 214 mg/dL (random).

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Cough improving; tingling feet; stopped tablets for 4 days fearing red urine; daily alcohol |
| **O** | Weight 46 kg (weight band checked); LFT normal; random glucose 214 mg/dL, HbA1c 8%; HIV negative |
| **A** | New pulmonary TB, intensive phase. DRPs: (1) **treatment interruption** due to misunderstanding of harmless rifampicin colour; (2) **isoniazid neuropathy** – pyridoxine needed; (3) **untreated diabetes** (worsens TB outcome); (4) alcohol – raises hepatotoxicity risk |
| **P** | Restart treatment at once (adherence support, treatment supporter); add pyridoxine; refer for diabetes management; alcohol cessation counselling; nutrition support (Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana); follow-up sputum at end of intensive phase as per programme; monitor LFT symptoms, vision, weight monthly |

**Counselling:** orange-red urine, sweat and tears are harmless; complete the full 6 months; take daily at the same time; report yellow eyes, vomiting, loss of appetite, blurred vision, rash; stop alcohol; cover mouth when coughing; screen family contacts.

## Result

A SOAP note for pulmonary TB was prepared; treatment interruption, isoniazid neuropathy, undiagnosed diabetes and alcohol use were identified and managed.

## Precautions

Check weight-band dose; never give a single anti-TB drug alone; notify the case; maintain confidentiality and avoid stigma.

## Viva questions

1. **NTEP regimen for drug-sensitive TB?** 2HRZE/4HRE daily.
2. **Why pyridoxine?** Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.
3. **Most hepatotoxic first-line drug?** Pyrazinamide.
4. **Which test detects rifampicin resistance quickly?** CBNAAT (GeneXpert) or TrueNat.
5. **Ethambutol toxicity?** Optic neuritis (red-green colour blindness).
practicals.title: SOAP note: tuberculosis

# SOAP note for a clinical case of anaemia (iron deficiency anaemia)

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of anaemia; iron deficiency anaemia is taken as the example (the same format suits megaloblastic anaemia).

## Principle

Iron deficiency anaemia is microcytic and hypochromic, confirmed by low ferritin. Management has two parts: replace iron (oral ferrous salts; IV iron if needed) and **find and treat the cause** (blood loss, hookworm, diet, pregnancy). Poor adherence because of GI upset and wrong timing with tea or calcium are common problems.

## Requirements

Case details, CBC with indices, serum ferritin, stool examination, prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record symptoms (fatigue, breathlessness, pica), menstrual history, diet, worm infestation, NSAID use, pregnancy.
2. Record pallor, koilonychia, Hb, MCV, MCH, ferritin, TIBC, stool for ova and occult blood.
3. Classify anaemia by severity and type; look for the cause.
4. Review the iron product (elemental iron content), timing and interactions.
5. Identify DRPs; plan therapy, monitoring and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Ms R, 17 years, student, tiredness, breathlessness on climbing stairs and craving to eat chalk. Heavy periods. Vegetarian. Started ferrous sulfate tablets but takes them with milk tea at breakfast; complains of constipation and black stools and wants to stop.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Fatigue, exertional breathlessness, pica, heavy periods, vegetarian diet; iron taken with tea; constipation; worried by black stools |
| **O** | Pallor, koilonychia; Hb 8.6 g/dL; MCV 68 fL; ferritin low; TIBC high; stool shows hookworm ova |
| **A** | Moderate iron deficiency anaemia due to menorrhagia, hookworm and low dietary iron. DRPs: (1) **reduced absorption** – iron taken with tea/milk; (2) **adverse effects** (constipation, black stools) leading to likely non-adherence; (3) **cause untreated** – hookworm, heavy periods |
| **P** | Take iron between meals or on an empty stomach with water/lemon juice (with food if upset); fluids and fibre for constipation; deworming with albendazole; gynaecology review for heavy periods; iron-rich diet; continue iron about 3 months after Hb is normal. Monitor Hb after 3–4 weeks (expect rise of about 1–2 g/dL) |

**Counselling:** black stools are expected and harmless; avoid tea, coffee and milk within about an hour of the tablet; vitamin C helps; continue the full course; keep tablets away from children; eat green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, ragi.

## Result

A SOAP note for iron deficiency anaemia was prepared; incorrect administration, adverse effects threatening adherence and untreated causes were identified and addressed.

## Precautions

Always look for the cause of iron deficiency; IV iron only where anaphylaxis can be treated; in megaloblastic anaemia never give folic acid alone if B12 deficiency is possible.

## Viva questions

1. **Best test for iron stores?** Serum ferritin.
2. **Expected Hb rise with oral iron?** About 1–2 g/dL in 3–4 weeks.
3. **What improves iron absorption?** Vitamin C.
4. **Antidote for iron poisoning?** Desferrioxamine.
5. **Common cause of IDA in Indian adolescents?** Heavy periods, poor diet, hookworm.
practicals.title: SOAP note: anaemia (iron deficiency)

# SOAP note for a clinical case of viral infection (COVID-19)

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a clinical case of a viral infection; mild COVID-19 is taken as the example (the same format suits influenza, herpes zoster or dengue).

## Principle

Most viral infections are self-limiting and need supportive care; specific antivirals exist only for some (oseltamivir for influenza, acyclovir for herpes, remdesivir in selected COVID-19 patients). Antibiotics do not act on viruses. In mild COVID-19 the key points are isolation, symptom relief, oxygen monitoring and recognising warning signs; steroids are not used in mild disease.

## Requirements

Case details, RT-PCR/antigen report, pulse oximeter, thermometer, prescription, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record symptoms, onset date, contacts, vaccination status, high-risk conditions (age, diabetes, hypertension, lung disease).
2. Record temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, SpO2, test result.
3. Classify severity (mild, moderate, severe).
4. Review the prescription for unnecessary drugs and interactions.
5. Identify DRPs; write plan, monitoring and counselling.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Mr G, 40 years, fever, sore throat and body ache for 2 days; RT-PCR positive for SARS-CoV-2. No breathlessness. Known diabetic on metformin. A local clinic prescribed azithromycin, dexamethasone tablets and multivitamins.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Fever, sore throat, myalgia for 2 days, no breathlessness; diabetic; fully vaccinated |
| **O** | Temperature 38.4 °C; pulse 96/min; respiratory rate 18/min; SpO2 97% on room air; random glucose 190 mg/dL |
| **A** | Mild COVID-19 in a diabetic. DRPs: (1) **unnecessary antibiotic** (no bacterial infection); (2) **steroid in mild disease** – no benefit, raises blood sugar and risk of fungal infection (mucormycosis); (3) need for sugar monitoring |
| **P** | Suggest to prescriber: stop azithromycin and dexamethasone; paracetamol for fever; fluids, rest, home isolation; monitor SpO2 and temperature 3–4 times a day and blood sugar daily; seek care if SpO2 below about 94%, breathlessness, chest pain or confusion; continue diabetes medicines |

**Counselling:** isolate and wear a mask at home; paracetamol for fever; drink fluids; check oxygen with the pulse oximeter (warm finger, rest, wait for a steady reading); antibiotics and steroids are not needed for mild illness; return immediately with warning signs; complete recommended vaccination.

## Result

A SOAP note for mild COVID-19 was prepared; unnecessary antibiotic and steroid use were identified and replaced with supportive care and monitoring.

## Precautions

Follow current national clinical guidance (it changes); infection-control measures during counselling; refer high-risk patients early.

## Viva questions

1. **Receptor used by SARS-CoV-2?** ACE2.
2. **When are steroids used in COVID-19?** In patients needing oxygen (moderate–severe), not in mild disease.
3. **Antiviral for influenza?** Oseltamivir.
4. **Pain-killers to avoid in dengue?** Aspirin and NSAIDs.
5. **Gold-standard test for COVID-19?** RT-PCR.
practicals.title: SOAP note: viral infection (COVID-19)

# SOAP note for a clinical case of a dermatological condition (scabies)

**Aim:** To prepare and discuss a SOAP note for a dermatological condition; scabies is taken as the example (the same format suits psoriasis or eczema).

## Principle

Scabies is a contagious mite infestation. Cure needs correct application of a scabicide (permethrin 5%) to the whole body, a repeat after a week, simultaneous treatment of all close contacts and washing of clothes and bedding. Most "treatment failures" are due to wrong application or untreated contacts.

## Requirements

Case details, prescription, scabicide demonstration tube, references, SOAP sheet.

## Procedure

1. Record itching (night-time), duration, affected family members, previous treatment and how it was applied.
2. Record lesion sites (burrows, papules), secondary infection.
3. Check the drug, method, amount and repeat schedule; check contacts' treatment.
4. Identify DRPs; plan and counsel.

## Observations (worked hypothetical case)

**Case:** Master T, 9 years, severe itching at night for 3 weeks; mother and sister also itch. Permethrin cream was applied only on the itchy spots once and washed off after 1 hour. Lesions are in finger webs, wrists and around the waist, some with crusts and pus.

| SOAP | Findings |
| --- | --- |
| **S** | Nocturnal itch for 3 weeks; family members itching; incorrect permethrin use (spots only, 1 hour, once) |
| **O** | Burrows and papules in finger webs, wrists, waist; a few pustules (secondary infection) |
| **A** | Scabies with secondary bacterial infection. DRPs: (1) **incorrect application** (area, contact time, no repeat); (2) **contacts untreated**; (3) infection not treated |
| **P** | Re-apply permethrin 5% to the whole body from the neck down, leave 8–12 hours (overnight), wash off, repeat after 7 days; treat mother and sister at the same time; antibiotic for infected lesions as prescribed; antihistamine at night for itch; hot-wash clothes and bedding |

**Counselling:** apply to cool, dry skin after a bath, covering finger webs, under nails, between toes and genitals; re-apply to hands if washed; all family members treated the same night; wash clothes, towels and bedding in hot water and dry in sun, or seal in a bag for 3 days; itching may continue for 2–4 weeks after cure – do not keep applying cream.

## Result

A SOAP note for scabies was prepared; incorrect application and untreated contacts were identified as causes of failure, and correct use was counselled.

## Precautions

Avoid lindane; oral ivermectin not for young children or pregnancy; check for crusted scabies in institutions.

## Viva questions

1. **Causative organism?** Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis.
2. **Drug of choice?** Permethrin 5% cream.
3. **Why repeat after 7 days?** To kill mites that hatch from eggs after the first application.
4. **Why treat contacts without itching?** They may be infested but not yet itchy (itch takes weeks to develop).
5. **Why does itching continue after treatment?** Allergic reaction to dead mites and their products.
practicals.title: SOAP note: dermatological condition (scabies)

# Patient counselling exercises using role plays

**Aim:** To practise and document patient counselling on the disease, medicines, life-style changes and monitoring parameters through role plays based on real or hypothetical cases (minimum five cases).

## Principle

Counselling is a two-way discussion that helps patients understand and follow their therapy. Good counselling uses simple language, open questions, demonstration where needed, checking understanding (**teach-back**) and written information. Role play lets students practise both as pharmacist and as patient, and the session is documented.

## Requirements

Case scenarios, prescriptions, demonstration devices (placebo inhalers, spacer, insulin pen, glucometer, eye drops), patient information leaflets, counselling documentation form, a quiet counselling area.

## Procedure

1. **Prepare:** read the case and prescription; list the key messages (about the disease, each drug, life-style, monitoring, warning signs).
2. **Open:** greet, introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the purpose and time needed, ensure privacy.
3. **Assess:** use open questions – "What did the doctor tell you about this medicine?", "How do you take it at home?" (the three prime questions: what is it for, how to take it, what to expect).
4. **Counsel:** explain the disease simply; for each drug – name, purpose, dose and timing, how to take, duration, common side effects and what to do, serious side effects to report, storage, interactions (food, alcohol, other medicines).
5. **Demonstrate** devices and ask the patient to show back.
6. **Life-style:** diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol, sleep as relevant.
7. **Monitoring:** what to check, how often, and follow-up dates.
8. **Close:** teach-back ("Can you tell me how you will take this?"), give written leaflet, invite questions, give contact details.
9. **Document** on the form: patient details, topics covered, devices demonstrated, barriers found, patient's understanding, follow-up.

## Observations: suggested five role-play cases with key points

| Case | Key counselling points |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Newly diagnosed hypertension on amlodipine | Silent disease; daily tablet even when well; ankle swelling possible; salt below 5 g/day, exercise, weight loss; home BP log; follow-up in 4 weeks |
| 2. Type 2 diabetes starting insulin pen | Storage (2–8 °C, not frozen), priming, injection sites and rotation, hypoglycaemia recognition and Rule of 15, foot care, glucometer use |
| 3. Asthma with MDI and spacer | Reliever vs preventer, technique with spacer, rinse after ICS, triggers, action plan |
| 4. Tuberculosis on FDC tablets | Full course, daily dosing, orange urine harmless, report jaundice/vision change, contraception, cough hygiene, nutrition |
| 5. Depression starting an SSRI | Not addictive, 2–4 weeks for effect, early nausea, do not stop suddenly, avoid alcohol, report suicidal thoughts |
| Optional: warfarin after stroke / glaucoma eye drops | Bleeding signs, INR, consistent diet / drop technique, nasolacrimal occlusion, lifelong use |

**Specimen documentation (case 1):**

| Item | Record |
| --- | --- |
| Patient | 50-year-old man, newly diagnosed hypertension |
| Medicines | Amlodipine once daily |
| Topics covered | Disease, purpose of drug, timing, ankle swelling, salt and exercise advice, home BP, follow-up |
| Teach-back | Correctly explained daily dosing and salt limit |
| Barriers | Forgets morning doses – advised pill box and phone alarm |
| Follow-up | BP review in 4 weeks |

## Result

Counselling sessions were conducted for at least five cases using role play, and the content, patient understanding and follow-up were documented.

## Precautions

Respect privacy and confidentiality; use the patient's language and avoid jargon; do not give information beyond your role – refer to the doctor when needed; be non-judgemental, especially for stigmatised conditions (HIV, TB, mental illness).

## Viva questions

1. **What is teach-back?** Asking the patient to explain or demonstrate in their own words to confirm understanding.
2. **Three prime questions?** What did the doctor tell you the medicine is for? How did the doctor tell you to take it? What did the doctor tell you to expect?
3. **Barriers to counselling?** Language, low literacy, hearing or vision problems, lack of time, privacy, stigma.
4. **Why written leaflets?** Patients forget much of verbal advice; leaflets reinforce it.
5. **What is discharge counselling?** Counselling at hospital discharge about medicines, devices, diet, warning signs and follow-up.
practicals.title: Patient counselling exercises using role plays
