# Unit 9: Infectious diseases II – gonorrhoea, syphilis, malaria, HIV and opportunistic infections, viral infections (SARS, COVID-19)

This unit is the second half of syllabus chapter 2(g). Many of these infections are treated under **national programmes** (malaria – National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control; HIV and sexually transmitted infections – National AIDS Control Programme), and the pharmacist must follow the programme regimens and counsel carefully because **stigma, adherence and partner treatment** decide success.

## 9.1 Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) – general points

- Spread mainly by unprotected sexual contact; one STI raises the risk of others, including HIV.
- India uses **syndromic management** in many clinics: treatment is based on the syndrome (urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, genital ulcer, lower abdominal pain) using **pre-packed STI kits**, so that patients are treated at the first visit.
- **Always:** treat the **partner(s)**, advise abstinence until both complete treatment, promote condoms, offer **HIV and syphilis testing**.

## 9.2 Gonorrhoea

### Definition and cause

**Gonorrhoea** is a sexually transmitted infection caused by ***Neisseria gonorrhoeae***, a **Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus**, which infects the mucous membranes of the urethra, cervix, rectum, throat and eye.

### Clinical manifestations

| In men | In women |
| --- | --- |
| **Purulent urethral discharge**, burning on urination, 2–7 days after exposure | Often **no symptoms**; vaginal discharge, burning urination, bleeding between periods |
| Complications: epididymitis, urethral stricture | Complications: **pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)**, ectopic pregnancy, **infertility** |

Others: proctitis, pharyngitis; **disseminated infection** (fever, joint pain, skin pustules); **ophthalmia neonatorum** – severe eye infection in newborns of infected mothers.

**Diagnosis:** Gram stain of discharge (Gram-negative diplococci inside pus cells), culture (also tests sensitivity), nucleic acid amplification tests.

### Management

- **Drug of choice:** a single dose of an injectable third-generation cephalosporin – **ceftriaxone IM** (cefixime orally is an alternative in some guidelines) – **plus azithromycin** (or doxycycline) to cover **chlamydia**, which often co-exists. Follow the national STI guideline for the exact regimen.
- Penicillin, tetracycline and fluoroquinolones are **no longer reliable** because of widespread resistance.
- Treat partners; test for HIV and syphilis; test of cure if symptoms persist.
- **Newborn:** eye prophylaxis and prompt treatment of ophthalmia neonatorum.

**Counselling:** complete the treatment; no sex until you and your partner(s) are treated and symptoms resolve; use condoms; return if discharge continues.

## 9.3 Syphilis

### Definition and cause

**Syphilis** is a chronic, multi-stage sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochaete ***Treponema pallidum***; it can also pass from mother to fetus (**congenital syphilis**) and rarely through blood.

### Stages and manifestations

| Stage | Time after infection | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary** | About 3 weeks (9–90 days) | **Painless, hard ulcer (chancre)** at the site of entry; painless swollen nodes; heals on its own |
| **Secondary** | 6 weeks – 6 months | Fever, malaise, **non-itchy rash including palms and soles**, mucous patches in mouth, condylomata lata (moist warty lesions), patchy hair loss |
| **Latent** | Years | No symptoms; only blood tests positive (early latent – infectious, late latent) |
| **Tertiary** | Many years | **Gummas** (destructive lesions of skin, bone), **cardiovascular** (aortitis, aneurysm), **neurosyphilis** (general paralysis, tabes dorsalis, dementia) |
| **Congenital** | — | Stillbirth, abortion; in babies: rash, snuffles, enlarged liver; later Hutchinson's teeth, saddle nose |

**Diagnosis:** dark-ground microscopy of chancre fluid; **non-treponemal tests** (VDRL, RPR – used for screening and to follow treatment response) and **treponemal tests** (TPHA, FTA-ABS – confirm infection; stay positive for life). All pregnant women are screened.

### Management

| Stage | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Early syphilis (primary, secondary, early latent) | **Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM, single dose** (given as two injections, one in each buttock) |
| Late latent / unknown duration / tertiary (not neuro) | Benzathine penicillin G **once weekly for 3 weeks** |
| Neurosyphilis | IV aqueous (crystalline) penicillin for about 2 weeks |
| Penicillin allergy (not pregnant) | Doxycycline (longer course) |
| **Pregnancy** | **Penicillin only** – desensitise if allergic (doxycycline is contraindicated) |

Test sensitivity to penicillin as per local practice and keep **anaphylaxis treatment ready**. **Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction:** fever, chills, headache and muscle pain within hours of the first dose, due to release of treponemal products; it settles in a day – treat with paracetamol and reassure.

**Follow-up:** repeat VDRL/RPR – a fourfold fall in titre shows response. **Counselling:** partner treatment; no sex until healed; condoms; return for follow-up tests; HIV test.

## 9.4 Malaria

### Definition and cause

**Malaria** is a **febrile illness** caused by **protozoa of the genus *Plasmodium***, transmitted by the bite of an infected **female *Anopheles* mosquito**. Species: ***P. vivax*** and ***P. falciparum*** (both common in India), *P. malariae*, *P. ovale*, *P. knowlesi*.

### Life cycle (simplified)

```text
Mosquito bite injects sporozoites
        ↓
Liver stage (hepatic schizogony) – no symptoms
   (P. vivax / P. ovale leave dormant HYPNOZOITES → relapse months later)
        ↓
Merozoites enter red blood cells → multiply → RBCs burst
        ↓                         (every 48 h: vivax, falciparum, ovale;
Fever paroxysm, anaemia             72 h: malariae)
        ↓
Some form gametocytes → taken up by a mosquito → cycle continues
```

### Clinical manifestations

- **Paroxysms:** **cold stage** (shivering, rigors) → **hot stage** (high fever, headache, vomiting) → **sweating stage** (fever falls); body aches, weakness.
- Enlarged spleen and liver, anaemia, mild jaundice.
- **Severe (complicated) malaria** – mostly ***P. falciparum*** (vivax can also be severe): **cerebral malaria** (altered consciousness, seizures, coma), severe anaemia, **hypoglycaemia**, jaundice, acute kidney injury, breathing difficulty (ARDS), shock, bleeding, high parasite count. High risk in children, pregnant women and non-immune travellers.

**Diagnosis:** **blood smear microscopy** (thick smear to detect, thin smear to identify species) or **rapid diagnostic test (RDT)**. Treat only confirmed cases.

### Drug management (Indian national guideline – summary)

| Situation | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| ***P. vivax*** | **Chloroquine for 3 days** + **primaquine daily for 14 days** (radical cure – kills hypnozoites, prevents relapse) |
| ***P. falciparum*** (uncomplicated) | **Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)** for 3 days: **artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (AS+SP)**; in the **north-eastern states** **artemether–lumefantrine (AL)** because of SP resistance; plus a **single dose of primaquine** (kills gametocytes – reduces spread) |
| Mixed infection | ACT + 14-day primaquine |
| **Severe malaria** | **Injectable artesunate (IV/IM)** for at least 24 hours (alternatives: IM artemether, IV quinine), then a full oral ACT course; manage glucose, fluids, fits, anaemia |
| Pregnancy | Treatment as per the national guideline for each trimester; **primaquine is not given** in pregnancy (or to infants) |

**Never use artemisinin alone (monotherapy)** – it encourages resistance. **Primaquine** can cause **haemolysis in G6PD deficiency** – check where possible and stop if urine turns dark.

**Other drugs:** quinine (tinnitus, low sugar – "cinchonism"), mefloquine (neuropsychiatric effects), doxycycline (used with quinine and for prophylaxis; not in children under 8 or pregnancy), atovaquone–proguanil.

### Prevention

- **Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs)**, indoor residual spraying, removing stagnant water, larvivorous fish.
- Personal protection: repellents, full-sleeved clothes, screens.
- **Chemoprophylaxis** for travellers to high-risk areas (doxycycline or mefloquine as advised).

### Counselling points

Complete all days of treatment even if fever goes; take tablets after food (less vomiting – repeat the dose if vomited within 30 minutes); report dark urine or yellow eyes during primaquine; return immediately if drowsy, fitting, unable to eat or very weak (signs of severe malaria); sleep under a treated bed net.

## 9.5 HIV infection and opportunistic infections

### Definition and cause

**HIV infection** is a chronic infection with the **human immunodeficiency virus** (a retrovirus: HIV-1, the common type, and HIV-2) that destroys **CD4+ T-lymphocytes**, leading to progressive immune deficiency. **AIDS** (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the advanced stage – **CD4 count below 200 cells/µL** or an **AIDS-defining illness**.

### Transmission

Unprotected sexual contact (most common), **mother to child** (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding), infected blood and blood products, **sharing needles** (injecting drug use), needle-stick injury. **Not** spread by touching, hugging, sharing food or utensils, or mosquitoes.

### Pathogenesis and stages

```text
HIV binds CD4 (+ CCR5/CXCR4) → enters cell → reverse transcriptase makes DNA
→ integrase inserts it into host DNA → new virus made (protease matures it)
        ↓
Acute infection (2–4 weeks): flu-like illness, high viral load
        ↓
Clinical latency (years): few symptoms, CD4 slowly falls
        ↓
AIDS: CD4 < 200 → opportunistic infections and cancers
```

**Clinical features of advanced disease:** weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, prolonged fever, oral thrush, swollen nodes, skin lesions, recurrent infections; **TB is the most common opportunistic infection in India**.

**Diagnosis:** antibody (and antigen) tests – in India **three tests with different principles** confirm infection in adults; **DNA PCR** in infants under 18 months; **CD4 count** and **viral load** for monitoring.

### Antiretroviral therapy (ART)

**Principle:** **"Treat all"** – ART is started for **every person diagnosed with HIV, regardless of CD4 count**, as early as possible, as a **combination of three drugs** (to prevent resistance), taken **lifelong**. ART is free at ART centres under the National AIDS Control Programme. The goal is an **undetectable viral load** – such a person does not pass HIV sexually ("Undetectable = Untransmittable").

| Class | Examples | Key adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **NRTIs** (nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors) | **Tenofovir (TDF)**, **lamivudine (3TC)**, emtricitabine, zidovudine (AZT), abacavir | Tenofovir – kidney damage, bone loss; zidovudine – **anaemia**; abacavir – hypersensitivity |
| **NNRTIs** | Efavirenz, nevirapine | Efavirenz – dizziness, vivid dreams; nevirapine – rash, hepatitis |
| **Integrase inhibitors (INSTIs)** | **Dolutegravir (DTG)**, raltegravir | Insomnia, weight gain; few interactions |
| **Protease inhibitors (PIs)** | Lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir/ritonavir, darunavir/ritonavir | GI upset, lipid and sugar changes, many interactions |

**Preferred first-line regimen in India for most adults and adolescents: TLD = tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir**, one tablet once daily. Adherence must be very high (about 95% or more of doses).

**Special situations:**
- **Prevention of parent-to-child transmission:** ART for all pregnant women with HIV; **nevirapine syrup prophylaxis for the infant**; safe delivery; infant testing.
- **Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP):** start **as soon as possible, within 72 hours**, continue for **28 days** (after needle-stick injury or sexual exposure).
- **Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP):** tenofovir-based drugs for high-risk HIV-negative people.
- **Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS):** worsening of an existing infection soon after starting ART as immunity recovers.
- **Drug interactions:** rifampicin lowers dolutegravir levels (dose adjustment needed); antacids and iron/calcium reduce dolutegravir absorption.

### Common opportunistic infections

| Infection | Treatment / prophylaxis |
| --- | --- |
| **Tuberculosis** | Standard anti-TB treatment + ART; TB preventive therapy for those without active TB |
| ***Pneumocystis jirovecii* pneumonia (PCP)** | **Cotrimoxazole** (high dose) ± steroids; **cotrimoxazole prophylaxis** in low CD4 or advanced disease (also prevents toxoplasmosis) |
| Oral / oesophageal **candidiasis** | Clotrimazole lozenges, nystatin, **fluconazole** |
| **Cryptococcal meningitis** | **Amphotericin B + flucytosine** (or fluconazole), then fluconazole maintenance |
| Cerebral toxoplasmosis | Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (+ folinic acid) or high-dose cotrimoxazole |
| CMV retinitis | Ganciclovir / valganciclovir |
| Herpes zoster, herpes simplex | **Acyclovir** |
| *Mycobacterium avium* complex | Clarithromycin/azithromycin + ethambutol |

### Counselling points

Take ART **every day at the same time, for life**; never share or stop drugs; use condoms; report side effects instead of stopping; take cotrimoxazole prophylaxis as advised; keep follow-up for CD4 and viral load; tell the doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines (interactions); maintain confidentiality and offer support against stigma.

## 9.6 Viral infections – SARS and COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2)

### Definitions

- **SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome)** is a severe viral pneumonia caused by **SARS-CoV**, a coronavirus that caused an outbreak in **2002–2003**, mainly in Asia; it was controlled by isolation and quarantine.
- **COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019)** is the illness caused by **SARS-CoV-2**, a new coronavirus first reported in late **2019**; WHO declared it a **pandemic in March 2020**.

### Etiopathogenesis of COVID-19

- Spread by **respiratory droplets and aerosols** (coughing, talking, especially in closed, crowded spaces), and less often contaminated surfaces.
- The virus uses its **spike protein** to bind the **ACE2 receptor** on cells of the respiratory tract and other organs.
- Severe disease involves an excessive immune response (**"cytokine storm"**), lung injury (ARDS) and a tendency to form **blood clots**.
- **Risk factors for severe disease:** old age, diabetes, hypertension, heart, lung and kidney disease, obesity, immunosuppression, being unvaccinated.

### Clinical manifestations

Fever, dry cough, sore throat, tiredness, body aches, headache, **loss of smell or taste**, diarrhoea; breathlessness and **low oxygen saturation** in moderate–severe disease. Many infections are mild or asymptomatic. Complications: pneumonia, ARDS, clots (stroke, pulmonary embolism), heart inflammation, secondary infections (including mucormycosis, seen in India especially with uncontrolled diabetes and steroid misuse), and long-lasting symptoms ("long COVID").

**Diagnosis:** **RT-PCR** of nasal/throat swab (gold standard), **rapid antigen test**; chest CT/X-ray, inflammatory markers in moderate–severe cases.

### Management (broad, following national clinical guidance)

| Severity | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Mild** (no breathlessness, normal oxygen) | **Home isolation**, rest, fluids, **paracetamol** for fever, monitor temperature and **oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter**; seek care if saturation falls (below about 94%), breathlessness, chest pain or confusion |
| **Moderate** (low oxygen) | Hospital; **oxygen**; **corticosteroids (dexamethasone)** for patients needing oxygen; **prophylactic anticoagulation** (enoxaparin/heparin); prone positioning |
| **Severe** | ICU; high-flow oxygen or ventilation; steroids, anticoagulation; antivirals (**remdesivir**) in selected patients; anti-IL-6 (**tocilizumab**) in selected cases |

**Not useful / not recommended:** antibiotics for the virus itself (only for proven bacterial infection), hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, convalescent plasma; **steroids should not be used in mild disease** (harm, mucormycosis risk). Oral antivirals (for example nirmatrelvir–ritonavir, molnupiravir) have been used in some high-risk patients – follow current guidance.

**Prevention:** **vaccination** (India used vaccines such as Covishield and Covaxin), masks in crowded indoor places, hand hygiene, ventilation, staying home when ill.

### Other common viral infections (for practicals)

| Infection | Specific treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Influenza | Oseltamivir (best within 48 hours of onset), annual vaccine |
| Herpes simplex, varicella–zoster (chickenpox, shingles) | Acyclovir, valacyclovir |
| Dengue | **No antiviral**; fluids and **paracetamol**; **avoid aspirin and NSAIDs** (bleeding) |
| Common cold | Symptomatic; antibiotics are not needed |

**Counselling (COVID-19):** isolate as advised; check oxygen regularly; take steroids only if prescribed and monitor sugar in diabetics; complete vaccination; seek help early for warning signs.

## Remember

- Gonorrhoea: Gram-negative diplococci; ceftriaxone + azithromycin (cover chlamydia); treat partners.
- Syphilis: painless chancre → rash on palms/soles → latent → tertiary; VDRL/RPR + TPHA; benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose for early syphilis; penicillin only in pregnancy; Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction.
- Malaria: vivax – chloroquine 3 days + primaquine 14 days; falciparum – ACT (AS+SP; AL in north-east) + single-dose primaquine; severe – injectable artesunate; no artemisinin monotherapy; G6PD and primaquine.
- HIV: treat all; TLD first-line; PEP within 72 h for 28 days; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis; TB is the commonest OI in India.
- COVID-19: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2; mild – home care, paracetamol, pulse oximetry; steroids and anticoagulants only for patients needing oxygen; vaccinate.

# Unit 10: Musculoskeletal and dermatological disorders

This unit joins two short syllabus parts: chapter 2(h) **musculoskeletal disorders** – rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis (3 hours) – and chapter 2(i) **dermatology** – psoriasis, scabies and eczema (3 hours). Comparing rheumatoid arthritis with osteoarthritis, and the three skin conditions with each other, is a favourite exam question.

## Part A: Musculoskeletal disorders

## 10.1 Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

### Definition

**Rheumatoid arthritis** is a **chronic, systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disease** that mainly affects the **synovial lining of joints**, causing **symmetrical polyarthritis** of small joints, which can lead to joint destruction, deformity and disability; it can also affect other organs.

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Cause:** not fully known – **genetic** tendency (HLA-DR4), **female sex** (about 2–3 times more common in women), **smoking**, possibly infections; usual onset 30–50 years.
- **Mechanism:**

```text
Trigger in a genetically prone person
        ↓
Autoimmune response (T cells, B cells → rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies)
        ↓
Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) → synovial inflammation and thickening (pannus)
        ↓
Pannus erodes cartilage and bone → joint deformity
```

### Clinical manifestations

- **Symmetrical** pain, swelling and tenderness of **small joints of hands and feet** (MCP, PIP, wrists, MTP); **distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are usually spared**.
- **Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour**, better with activity.
- Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, anaemia.
- Late deformities: **ulnar deviation**, **swan-neck** and **boutonnière** deformities.
- Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, dry eyes, lung fibrosis, vasculitis, higher risk of heart disease.

**Investigations:** raised ESR and CRP; **rheumatoid factor** and **anti-CCP antibodies** (anti-CCP is more specific); X-ray (erosions, narrowing); anaemia of chronic disease.

### Goals

Relieve pain and inflammation, **stop joint damage**, maintain function and quality of life – aiming for **remission or low disease activity ("treat to target")**.

### Non-drug management

Patient education; rest during flares and **regular exercise and physiotherapy** between flares; splints; occupational therapy; weight control; **stop smoking**; balanced diet; surgery (joint replacement) for damaged joints.

### Drug management

**Key principle:** start a **disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) early** – within the first few months – because joint damage happens early. NSAIDs and steroids relieve symptoms but **do not stop damage**.

| Group | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Conventional DMARDs** | **Methotrexate** (anchor drug, weekly), hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide | Take weeks to months to act; can be combined |
| **Biologic DMARDs** | Anti-TNF: **infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept**; tocilizumab (anti-IL-6); rituximab; abatacept | When conventional DMARDs fail; screen for **TB and hepatitis B** first; infection risk |
| Targeted synthetic DMARDs | Tofacitinib (JAK inhibitor) | Oral |
| **NSAIDs** | Ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, etoricoxib | Symptom relief only; GI, kidney, CV risks |
| **Corticosteroids** | Prednisolone (low dose, short "bridge"), intra-articular injection | Rapid relief while DMARDs start working |

**Methotrexate counselling and monitoring:**
- Taken **once a week on the same day – never daily** (daily dosing by mistake has caused deaths).
- **Folic acid** is given on another day to reduce side effects (mouth ulcers, nausea).
- Regular **blood counts, liver and kidney tests**; avoid alcohol.
- **Contraindicated in pregnancy** (teratogenic) – use contraception (men and women).
- Avoid cotrimoxazole and high-dose NSAIDs without advice (raise toxicity).
- Report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, breathlessness or bruising.

Hydroxychloroquine needs regular **eye examinations** (retinal toxicity). Sulfasalazine may colour urine orange.

## 10.2 Osteoarthritis (OA)

### Definition

**Osteoarthritis** is a **chronic degenerative joint disease** characterised by **progressive loss of articular cartilage**, with new bone formation (osteophytes) at the joint margins and changes in the underlying bone, leading to pain and stiffness, mainly in **weight-bearing joints**. It is the **most common form of arthritis**.

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Risk factors:** **increasing age**, **obesity** (major, especially for knees), female sex (after menopause), previous joint injury, repeated joint stress (occupation, squatting), joint deformity, family history.
- **Mechanism:** wear and repair imbalance – cartilage chondrocytes cannot keep up with damage → cartilage thins and cracks → bone rubs on bone → bone hardens (sclerosis), forms osteophytes and cysts → secondary mild inflammation.

### Clinical manifestations

- Joint **pain that increases with use and is relieved by rest**; worse at the end of the day.
- **Short morning stiffness (less than 30 minutes)** and stiffness after rest ("gelling").
- **Crepitus** (grating sound), reduced movement, bony swelling, deformity (bow legs).
- Commonly affected: **knees, hips**, spine, **DIP joints** (Heberden's nodes), PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes), base of thumb.
- No systemic features; ESR, CRP and rheumatoid factor normal. X-ray: joint-space narrowing, osteophytes.

### Rheumatoid arthritis vs osteoarthritis

| Feature | Rheumatoid arthritis | Osteoarthritis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Autoimmune, inflammatory | Degenerative ("wear and tear") |
| Age | Any, often 30–50 years | Usually above 50 years |
| Joints | Small joints of hands/feet, symmetrical; DIP spared | Large weight-bearing joints (knee, hip); DIP involved |
| Morning stiffness | More than 1 hour | Less than 30 minutes |
| Systemic features | Fever, fatigue, anaemia, nodules | Absent |
| Blood tests | Raised ESR/CRP; RF and anti-CCP positive | Normal |
| X-ray | Erosions, periarticular osteopenia | Joint-space narrowing, osteophytes |
| Main treatment | DMARDs (methotrexate) | Exercise, weight loss, analgesics |

### Management of OA

**Non-drug (the foundation):**
1. **Weight reduction** – reduces knee load and pain.
2. **Exercise** – quadriceps strengthening, low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming); physiotherapy.
3. Walking stick (in the hand opposite the painful knee or hip), knee braces, proper footwear.
4. Avoid squatting, sitting cross-legged and climbing too many stairs; hot or cold packs.
5. **Total joint replacement** for severe disease.

**Drugs:**

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Topical NSAIDs** (diclofenac gel) | First choice for knee and hand OA, especially in the elderly – fewer systemic side effects |
| Paracetamol | Safe and cheap, but modest effect; respect the maximum daily dose |
| Oral NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or COX-2 inhibitors (etoricoxib, celecoxib) | Lowest dose, shortest time; with PPI if GI risk; avoid in kidney disease, heart failure |
| Duloxetine | For chronic pain in some patients |
| Topical capsaicin | Burning at first; helps some |
| **Intra-articular corticosteroid** | Short-term relief of a painful flare |
| Intra-articular hyaluronic acid | Modest, variable benefit |
| Glucosamine, chondroitin | Evidence weak and inconsistent |
| Tramadol / opioids | Only when other measures fail; risk of falls, dependence |

**Counselling:** lose weight and keep exercising – these work better than many drugs; use NSAIDs only as advised with food; wash hands after applying gels; report black stools or swelling of legs.

## Part B: Dermatological disorders

## 10.3 Psoriasis

### Definition

**Psoriasis** is a **chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory skin disease** characterised by **well-defined red plaques covered with silvery-white scales**, due to rapid skin-cell turnover; it runs a course of remissions and relapses and is **not contagious**.

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Genetic** tendency (family history); **T-cell–mediated** inflammation (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) → skin cells mature in a few days instead of about 4 weeks → thick scaly plaques.
- **Triggers:** stress, streptococcal throat infection (guttate psoriasis), skin injury (**Koebner phenomenon** – lesions appear at injured sites), cold dry weather, smoking, alcohol, obesity; **drugs – lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine), NSAIDs, sudden withdrawal of systemic steroids**.

### Clinical manifestations

- **Plaque psoriasis** (most common): raised red plaques with silvery scales on **elbows, knees, scalp, lower back**; may itch.
- **Auspitz sign** – pinpoint bleeding when scales are scraped off.
- Nail changes: **pitting**, thickening, separation (onycholysis).
- Other forms: guttate (drop-like), pustular, erythrodermic (whole body – emergency), flexural.
- **Psoriatic arthritis** in some patients; higher risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease and depression.

### Management

**Non-drug:** **emollients and moisturisers** daily; avoid triggers; gentle bathing; reduce stress, alcohol and smoking; weight loss; controlled sunlight.

**Topical (mild–moderate disease):**

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Topical corticosteroids** | Mainstay; potency by site (mild on face and folds); limit long-term use (skin thinning) |
| **Vitamin D analogues** (calcipotriol) | Often combined with a steroid |
| Coal tar | Messy, smelly; stains clothes |
| **Salicylic acid** | Removes scales (keratolytic), helps other drugs penetrate |
| Dithranol | Short-contact therapy; stains and irritates normal skin |
| Tacrolimus | Face and flexures |

**Phototherapy:** narrow-band UVB; PUVA (psoralen + UVA).

**Systemic (moderate–severe):** **methotrexate**, ciclosporin, acitretin (strongly **teratogenic** – avoid pregnancy for years after stopping), apremilast, and **biologics** (adalimumab, etanercept, secukinumab, ustekinumab). **Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided** – stopping them can cause severe pustular or erythrodermic flares.

**Counselling:** psoriasis is not infectious; use moisturiser daily; apply topical steroids thinly as directed and do not overuse; coal tar and dithranol stain; expect long-term control rather than cure.

## 10.4 Scabies

### Definition

**Scabies** is a **contagious, intensely itchy skin infestation** caused by the mite ***Sarcoptes scabiei* var. *hominis***, which burrows into the upper layer of the skin.

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Spread by close, prolonged skin-to-skin contact** (family members, hostels, overcrowded homes, sexual contact); less often through shared clothes and bedding.
- The female mite burrows and lays eggs; itching is due to an **allergic reaction** to mites, eggs and faeces, which takes 2–6 weeks to develop in a first infection (so contacts may be infected without itching yet).
- **Crusted (Norwegian) scabies:** thousands of mites in elderly, immunocompromised or disabled people – very contagious.

### Clinical manifestations

- **Severe itching, worse at night**; often several family members itch.
- **Burrows** (short wavy lines) and small papules, vesicles in **finger webs, wrists, elbows, armpits, around the waist and navel, genitals, buttocks, around nipples**; in infants also palms, soles and scalp.
- Secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) from scratching.

### Management

**Treat the patient and ALL household and close contacts at the same time**, even without symptoms.

| Drug | Use |
| --- | --- |
| **Permethrin 5% cream** | **First choice**; apply to the **whole body from the neck down** (include head and face in infants and the elderly), leave for **8–12 hours** (overnight), then wash off; **repeat after 7 days** |
| **Ivermectin (oral)** | Two doses about a week apart; useful for crusted scabies, institutions, or when topical treatment is difficult; not in young children or pregnancy |
| Benzyl benzoate 25% lotion | Alternative; irritant; diluted for children |
| Crotamiton, sulphur ointment | Alternatives (sulphur ointment is safe in infants and pregnancy) |
| Lindane | Not preferred – neurotoxicity |

**Supportive:** antihistamines (for example cetirizine) or calamine for itch; antibiotics if infected.

**Counselling:**
1. Apply to cool, dry skin after a bath; cover all areas including under nails, between fingers and toes; re-apply to hands if washed.
2. **Wash clothes, towels and bedding in hot water** and dry in the sun on the day of treatment; items that cannot be washed should be kept sealed in a bag for about 3 days.
3. **Itching may continue for 2–4 weeks** after successful treatment – do not keep re-applying permethrin; use antihistamines.
4. Return if new burrows appear after the second application.

## 10.5 Eczema (dermatitis)

### Definition

**Eczema** (used here interchangeably with dermatitis) is an **inflammatory skin condition** with itching, redness, scaling and, in acute stages, oozing vesicles; **atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis)** is the most common type, a chronic relapsing condition often starting in childhood.

### Types

| Type | Cause / features |
| --- | --- |
| **Atopic dermatitis** | Genetic **skin-barrier defect (filaggrin)** + immune tendency; family or personal history of asthma, hay fever; flexures of elbows and knees, face in infants |
| Contact dermatitis – irritant | Repeated detergents, soaps, water (hands of housewives, cleaners) |
| Contact dermatitis – allergic | Type IV allergy to nickel (jewellery), hair dye, rubber, cosmetics, topical medicines |
| Seborrhoeic dermatitis | Scalp (dandruff), face, chest; *Malassezia* yeast |
| Others | Nummular (coin-shaped), dyshidrotic (vesicles on palms), stasis (legs with varicose veins) |

### Clinical manifestations

**Intense itching** (the itch–scratch cycle), dry skin, red patches; acute – oozing, crusting; chronic – thick, darkened, leathery skin (**lichenification**). Infection with *Staphylococcus aureus* or herpes simplex can complicate it.

### Management

**Non-drug (most important):**
- **Emollients** liberally and often (after bathing, on damp skin) – the foundation of treatment.
- **Soap substitutes**, lukewarm short baths; avoid harsh soaps, wool, tight synthetic clothes, overheating.
- **Avoid irritants and identified allergens** (patch testing for contact dermatitis); wear gloves.
- Keep nails short; manage stress.

**Drugs:**

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Topical corticosteroids** | Mainstay for flares; choose potency for site and age (mild on face and in children), short courses |
| **Topical calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) | Face, eyelids, flexures; steroid-sparing |
| Oral antihistamines | Sedating ones (for example hydroxyzine) at night help itch and sleep |
| Antibiotics / antivirals | For infected eczema |
| Systemic therapy (severe) | Short oral steroids (rarely), ciclosporin, methotrexate, azathioprine, **dupilumab** (biologic), phototherapy |

**Fingertip unit (FTU):** the amount of cream squeezed from a standard tube along the last segment of an adult index finger – enough for an area about two adult palms; helps patients apply the right amount of steroid.

**Counselling:** use emollients every day, even when the skin is clear; apply the steroid thinly and only as long as advised (overuse thins skin; stopping suddenly after long use can cause flares); avoid triggers; it is not contagious.

### Psoriasis vs eczema vs scabies

| Feature | Psoriasis | Eczema | Scabies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Immune, rapid cell turnover | Barrier defect, allergy, irritants | Mite infestation |
| Contagious | No | No | **Yes** |
| Lesion | Sharp red plaques, silvery scale | Ill-defined red, dry, oozing or thick patches | Burrows, papules |
| Sites | Elbows, knees, scalp | Flexures, hands, face | Finger webs, wrists, waist, genitals |
| Itch | Mild–moderate | Severe | Severe, worse at night |
| Key treatment | Topical steroid + calcipotriol; methotrexate, biologics | Emollients + topical steroid | Permethrin 5% for patient and contacts |

## Remember

- RA: autoimmune, symmetrical small joints, morning stiffness more than 1 hour, RF and anti-CCP; start methotrexate early (weekly, with folic acid, not in pregnancy).
- OA: degenerative, weight-bearing joints, pain on use, stiffness less than 30 minutes; weight loss + exercise first; topical NSAIDs; paracetamol.
- Psoriasis: silvery plaques, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon; topical steroids + calcipotriol; avoid systemic steroids; lithium and beta-blockers can trigger it.
- Scabies: *Sarcoptes scabiei*; itch worse at night; permethrin 5% neck down, 8–12 hours, repeat after 7 days; treat all contacts; hot-wash bedding.
- Eczema: emollients daily are the foundation; topical steroids for flares; tacrolimus for face.

# Unit 11: Psychiatric disorders – depression, anxiety and psychosis

Syllabus chapter 2(j), 4 hours. Mental illnesses are common, under-treated and surrounded by stigma. The pharmacist's role is to explain that the drugs work **slowly**, are **not addictive** (except benzodiazepines), must **not be stopped suddenly**, and to watch for side effects and **suicide risk**.

## 11.1 Depression (major depressive disorder)

### Definition

**Depression** is a **mood disorder** with a **persistent low mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure** in usual activities, together with other symptoms, lasting **at least 2 weeks**, that cause distress or impair daily functioning. It is different from ordinary short-term sadness.

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Biological:** **monoamine hypothesis** – reduced activity of **serotonin (5-HT), noradrenaline and dopamine** in the brain; also stress-hormone (HPA axis) over-activity and reduced neuroplasticity (BDNF); **genetic** tendency (family history).
- **Psychosocial:** stressful life events (loss, unemployment, debt), childhood adversity, loneliness, chronic illness, postpartum period.
- **Medical causes:** hypothyroidism, Parkinson's disease, stroke, cancer, chronic pain, alcohol and substance use.
- **Drugs:** corticosteroids, reserpine, beta-blockers (rarely), oral contraceptives (some women), isotretinoin, interferon, alcohol.

### Clinical manifestations

The two core symptoms are **low mood** and **loss of interest (anhedonia)**. Others (remember "SIG E CAPS"):

| Letter | Symptom |
| --- | --- |
| S | **Sleep** disturbance (insomnia, early-morning waking, or excess sleep) |
| I | Loss of **interest** |
| G | **Guilt**, feelings of worthlessness |
| E | Low **energy**, fatigue |
| C | Poor **concentration**, indecision |
| A | **Appetite** change, weight loss or gain |
| P | **Psychomotor** slowing or agitation |
| S | **Suicidal** thoughts |

Severity: mild, moderate, severe (with or without psychotic features). Screening tools: PHQ-9, Hamilton rating scale.

### Management

**Non-drug:** psychoeducation; **psychotherapy** – cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), interpersonal therapy (first choice for mild depression, combined with drugs in moderate–severe); regular exercise, sleep hygiene, avoiding alcohol; social support; **electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)** for severe, suicidal, psychotic or treatment-resistant depression.

**Drug management:**

| Class | Examples | Key adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SSRIs** (first choice) | **Fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram**, paroxetine | Nausea, headache, insomnia or drowsiness, **sexual dysfunction**, low sodium (elderly), bleeding risk with NSAIDs/anticoagulants; agitation early in treatment |
| SNRIs | Venlafaxine, duloxetine | As SSRIs + raised BP |
| **Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs)** | Amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline | **Anticholinergic** (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision), sedation, postural hypotension, weight gain, **cardiotoxic in overdose (dangerous)** |
| Atypical | Mirtazapine (sedation, weight gain), bupropion (no sexual side effects; lowers seizure threshold), trazodone, vortioxetine | — |
| MAO inhibitors | Phenelzine, moclobemide | **Cheese (tyramine) reaction** – hypertensive crisis; many interactions; rarely used |

**Principles of antidepressant therapy:**
1. Benefit begins in **2–4 weeks**, full effect in **4–8 weeks**; side effects appear earlier – warn the patient.
2. Start low (especially in elderly), adjust after an adequate trial (4–6 weeks at a proper dose).
3. After remission, **continue for at least 6–12 months** to prevent relapse (longer for recurrent depression).
4. **Taper slowly** when stopping – sudden stopping causes a **discontinuation syndrome** (dizziness, "electric shock" sensations, irritability, flu-like symptoms), especially with paroxetine and venlafaxine.
5. **Serotonin syndrome** (agitation, sweating, tremor, high temperature, muscle jerks) can occur when serotonergic drugs are combined (SSRI + MAOI, tramadol, linezolid, triptans).
6. Young people (under about 25) may have **more suicidal thoughts early in treatment** – close monitoring; dispense limited quantities if suicide risk is high.
7. In **bipolar disorder**, antidepressants alone can trigger mania – mood stabilisers (lithium, valproate) are needed.

**Counselling:** "These medicines are not habit-forming and take a few weeks to work – keep taking them"; do not stop without advice; avoid alcohol; report worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm immediately (helpline / doctor); take SSRIs in the morning if they disturb sleep.

## 11.2 Anxiety disorders

### Definition

**Anxiety** is a normal emotional response to threat. An **anxiety disorder** exists when anxiety is **excessive, persistent, out of proportion to the situation and interferes with daily life**.

### Types

| Disorder | Features |
| --- | --- |
| **Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)** | Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many everyday matters for 6 months or more, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance |
| **Panic disorder** | Recurrent sudden **panic attacks** – palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, sweating, trembling, fear of dying – peaking within minutes; fear of further attacks |
| Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) | Fear of being judged in social or performance situations |
| Specific phobia | Fear of a particular object or situation (heights, animals) |
| Related conditions | Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) |

### Etiopathogenesis

Genetic tendency; imbalance of **GABA** (reduced inhibition), **serotonin** and **noradrenaline**; over-active amygdala (fear centre); stressful life events, personality, childhood trauma; **medical causes** (hyperthyroidism, arrhythmias, low sugar, asthma) and **substances** (caffeine, nicotine, alcohol withdrawal, salbutamol, steroids, thyroxine excess) must be excluded.

### Clinical manifestations

**Psychological:** worry, fear, restlessness, irritability, poor concentration, sleep problems. **Physical (autonomic):** palpitations, fast breathing, sweating, tremor, dry mouth, butterflies in the stomach, frequent urination, diarrhoea, headache, muscle tension.

### Management

**Non-drug:** **CBT** (first-line, with lasting benefit), relaxation and breathing exercises, yoga, meditation, regular exercise, reduce caffeine and alcohol, sleep hygiene.

**Drug management:**

| Drug | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **SSRIs** (escitalopram, sertraline, paroxetine) and **SNRIs** (venlafaxine, duloxetine) | **First-line long-term treatment** for GAD, panic and social anxiety; take 2–4 weeks or more to act; continue about 6–12 months after improvement |
| **Benzodiazepines** (alprazolam, lorazepam, clonazepam, diazepam) | **Short-term only (2–4 weeks)** for severe distress, or while SSRI starts working; **risk of dependence, tolerance, withdrawal**, sedation, falls, impaired driving; dangerous with alcohol and opioids |
| Buspirone | GAD; not sedating, no dependence; slow onset |
| Pregabalin | GAD in some guidelines |
| **Propranolol** | Controls physical symptoms (tremor, palpitations) in **performance anxiety**; avoid in asthma |
| Hydroxyzine | Sedating antihistamine, short-term |

**Counselling:** benzodiazepines are for short use only; do not drive or drink alcohol; do not stop them suddenly after regular use (withdrawal – anxiety, insomnia, even seizures); SSRIs may increase anxiety for the first week or two before helping; practise breathing exercises during panic.

## 11.3 Psychosis (with emphasis on schizophrenia)

### Definition

**Psychosis** is a mental state in which a person **loses contact with reality**, shown by **hallucinations** (perceiving things that are not there, commonly hearing voices) and **delusions** (fixed false beliefs not in keeping with the person's culture), often with disorganised thinking and behaviour. **Schizophrenia** is the commonest chronic psychotic disorder; psychosis also occurs in bipolar mania, severe depression, dementia, delirium and drug abuse (cannabis, amphetamines, alcohol withdrawal) and with some drugs (high-dose steroids, levodopa).

### Etiopathogenesis

- **Dopamine hypothesis:** **excess dopamine activity in the mesolimbic pathway** produces positive symptoms; reduced dopamine in the mesocortical pathway may cause negative and cognitive symptoms. Glutamate (NMDA) and serotonin systems are also involved.
- **Genetic** risk (family history), problems in brain development (birth complications), **cannabis use**, urban stress, migration, social adversity.

### Clinical manifestations of schizophrenia

| Group | Features |
| --- | --- |
| **Positive symptoms** | **Hallucinations** (voices commenting or commanding), **delusions** (persecution, reference, grandeur, thought insertion/broadcasting), disorganised speech and behaviour, agitation |
| **Negative symptoms** | Flat emotions, poverty of speech, lack of motivation, social withdrawal, self-neglect |
| **Cognitive symptoms** | Poor attention, memory and planning |

Lack of insight is common; onset usually in late teens to early 30s; relapse often follows stopping medicines.

### Management

**Non-drug:** psychoeducation of patient and family, supportive therapy, CBT for psychosis, **family therapy**, social skills and vocational training, community support, adherence support; hospital admission for risk to self or others; ECT in selected cases (catatonia, severe illness).

**Drug management – antipsychotics:**

| Group | Examples | Main adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Typical (first-generation)** – D2 blockers | **Haloperidol**, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine, trifluoperazine | **Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS)**: acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, **tardive dyskinesia**; high prolactin; sedation and hypotension (chlorpromazine) |
| **Atypical (second-generation)** – D2 + 5-HT2A blockers | **Risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole**, ziprasidone | **Metabolic effects** – weight gain, diabetes, raised lipids (most with olanzapine and clozapine); less EPS; risperidone – high prolactin |
| **Clozapine** | — | For **treatment-resistant schizophrenia**; risk of **agranulocytosis** – regular blood counts required; seizures, myocarditis, constipation, drooling |
| Long-acting (depot) injections | Fluphenazine decanoate, haloperidol decanoate, paliperidone palmitate | For poor adherence |

**Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS):** rare, life-threatening – high fever, **severe muscle rigidity**, confusion, unstable BP, high CPK; stop the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate, dantrolene/bromocriptine in hospital.

**Management of EPS:** acute dystonia and parkinsonism – anticholinergics (**trihexyphenidyl, IM promethazine or biperiden**); akathisia – propranolol or dose reduction; tardive dyskinesia – may be permanent; prevention by lowest effective dose and atypical drugs.

**Principles:** improvement in agitation within days, but positive symptoms take weeks; use **one antipsychotic at the lowest effective dose**; after a first episode continue for **at least 1–2 years**, longer after relapses; **monitor weight, waist, blood sugar, lipids, BP** (atypicals), and prolactin-related effects.

**Acute agitation:** oral or IM haloperidol, olanzapine or lorazepam (often haloperidol + promethazine IM in Indian practice).

**Counselling (often to the family):** the illness is treatable and relapse is common if medicines are stopped; continue medicines even when well; report stiffness, abnormal movements, high fever, or (with clozapine) sore throat and fever; healthy diet and exercise to limit weight gain; avoid alcohol and cannabis; do not drive if drowsy.

## 11.4 Quick comparison

| Feature | Depression | Anxiety | Psychosis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Core problem | Low mood, loss of interest | Excessive fear and worry | Loss of contact with reality |
| Neurotransmitters | ↓ 5-HT, NA | ↓ GABA, 5-HT/NA imbalance | ↑ Dopamine (mesolimbic) |
| First-line drugs | SSRIs | SSRIs/SNRIs (benzodiazepines short-term) | Atypical or typical antipsychotics |
| Onset of drug benefit | 2–4 weeks | 2–4 weeks (benzodiazepines quick) | Days to weeks |
| Key risk | Suicide, discontinuation syndrome | Benzodiazepine dependence | EPS, metabolic effects, NMS, agranulocytosis (clozapine) |
| Psychotherapy | CBT, interpersonal therapy | CBT | Family therapy, CBT for psychosis |

## Remember

- Depression: 2 weeks of low mood/anhedonia; SSRIs first; effect in 2–4 weeks; continue 6–12 months after remission; taper; watch suicide risk and serotonin syndrome.
- Anxiety: CBT + SSRI/SNRI long term; benzodiazepines only 2–4 weeks; propranolol for performance anxiety.
- Psychosis: hallucinations and delusions; dopamine excess; typical antipsychotics → EPS; atypicals → weight gain and diabetes; clozapine for resistant cases with blood counts; NMS is an emergency.
- Never stop psychiatric medicines suddenly; involve the family in counselling.

# Unit 12: Ophthalmic disorders and antimicrobial resistance

This unit joins two short syllabus parts of 2 hours each: chapter 2(k) **ophthalmology** – conjunctivitis (bacterial and viral) and glaucoma – and chapter 2(l) **antimicrobial resistance (AMR)**. They are kept together because both are short; the conjunctivitis section is also a good example of where antibiotics are often used when they are not needed.

## Part A: Ophthalmology

## 12.1 Conjunctivitis

### Definition

**Conjunctivitis** ("pink eye", "eye flu") is **inflammation of the conjunctiva** – the thin transparent membrane covering the white of the eye and the inner surface of the eyelids – causing redness, discharge and discomfort. It may be **infective** (bacterial, viral) or **non-infective** (allergic, irritant).

### Etiopathogenesis

| Type | Causes | Spread |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bacterial** | *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*; in newborns *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* and *Chlamydia trachomatis* (ophthalmia neonatorum) | Contact with hands, towels, cosmetics |
| **Viral** (most common infective type in adults) | **Adenovirus** (epidemic keratoconjunctivitis), enterovirus (acute haemorrhagic conjunctivitis outbreaks), herpes simplex, varicella-zoster | Highly contagious – hands, towels, droplets, swimming pools; outbreaks in monsoon |
| Allergic | Pollen, dust, animal dander; vernal keratoconjunctivitis in children | Not contagious |

### Clinical manifestations

| Feature | Bacterial | Viral | Allergic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discharge | **Thick, purulent (yellow-green)**; lids stuck together in the morning | **Watery** | Watery, stringy |
| Itching | Mild | Mild | **Marked** |
| Eyes | Often one eye first, then both | Often starts in one eye, spreads to the other; recent cold or sore throat | Both eyes |
| Lymph node | Usually none | **Tender pre-auricular node** | None |
| Other | — | Grittiness, light sensitivity, may last 1–3 weeks | Sneezing, hay fever, seasonal |

**Red flags (refer to an eye specialist):** **reduced vision**, severe eye pain, marked light sensitivity, a cloudy cornea, unequal pupils, contact-lens wearer with red painful eye, newborn with discharge, injury or chemical splash – these may be keratitis, uveitis or acute glaucoma, not simple conjunctivitis.

### Management

**General / non-drug (all infective types):**
- **Hand washing**; do not touch or rub eyes; **separate towel, pillow and handkerchief**; avoid crowded places, school or work until discharge settles.
- Clean the eyelids with boiled-and-cooled water and clean cotton, wiping from inside to outside, one swab per wipe.
- Cold compresses for comfort; stop contact lenses until fully recovered and discard the old lenses/case; avoid eye make-up.
- **Do not use steroid eye drops without an eye specialist** – steroids can worsen herpes infection and cause glaucoma and cataract.

**Bacterial conjunctivitis:**
- Often settles in a week even without treatment; **topical antibiotics** shorten the illness: **moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, gatifloxacin, chloramphenicol, tobramycin** eye drops (ointment at night or for children), usually 5–7 days.
- **Ophthalmia neonatorum** – systemic treatment (for example ceftriaxone for gonococcal, oral azithromycin/erythromycin for chlamydial) + eye care; urgent.

**Viral conjunctivitis:**
- **No antibiotic is needed** – it is self-limiting; supportive care: cold compresses, **lubricating eye drops (artificial tears)**, paracetamol for discomfort, strict hygiene.
- **Herpes simplex** conjunctivitis/keratitis: topical **acyclovir** or ganciclovir gel under specialist care; no steroids.

**Allergic:** avoid the allergen, cold compresses, **antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops** (olopatadine, ketotifen, sodium cromoglicate), oral antihistamines.

### Counselling on using eye drops

1. Wash hands; tilt head back; pull down the lower lid to make a pocket.
2. Instil **one drop**; do not let the dropper tip touch the eye or lashes.
3. Close the eye gently for 1–2 minutes and press the inner corner (**nasolacrimal occlusion**) – keeps the drug in the eye and reduces absorption into the body.
4. Wait **5 minutes between different drops**; apply ointment last.
5. **Discard opened eye drops after 4 weeks** (or as labelled); never share.

## 12.2 Glaucoma

### Definition

**Glaucoma** is a group of eye diseases characterised by **progressive damage to the optic nerve (optic neuropathy)** with **characteristic loss of the visual field**, usually associated with **raised intraocular pressure (IOP)**. Normal IOP is about **10–21 mmHg**. Lost vision **cannot be restored**, so early detection is vital – glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness ("silent thief of sight").

### Physiology and pathogenesis

```text
Aqueous humour made by ciliary body
        ↓
Flows through pupil into the anterior chamber
        ↓
Drains through trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm (main route)
          and uveoscleral route (second route)

Drainage blocked or reduced → aqueous builds up → ↑ IOP
        ↓
Pressure + poor blood supply damage optic nerve → cupping of the optic disc
        ↓
Peripheral vision lost first (tunnel vision) → blindness
```

### Types

| Type | Features |
| --- | --- |
| **Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)** – most common | Angle is open but drainage through the meshwork is poor; **slow, painless**, no symptoms until late; gradual loss of side vision |
| **Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG)** – **acute attack is an emergency** | Iris blocks the drainage angle (narrow angles, more common in Asians, hypermetropes, elderly women); **sudden severe eye pain, headache, red eye, blurred vision, haloes around lights, nausea and vomiting**, hazy cornea, mid-dilated fixed pupil |
| Normal-tension glaucoma | Optic nerve damage with IOP in normal range |
| **Secondary glaucoma** | Due to **long-term corticosteroids** (eye drops, oral, inhaled), uveitis, injury, cataract, diabetes (neovascular) |
| Congenital glaucoma | In infants – large, cloudy eyes, watering |

**Risk factors:** age above 40, family history, high myopia (open-angle) or hypermetropia (angle-closure), diabetes, hypertension, long-term steroid use, African or Asian descent.

**Drugs that can precipitate angle-closure** in people with narrow angles: **anticholinergics** (atropine, ipratropium nebulisation, TCAs), **antihistamines**, **adrenergic** drugs, topiramate, mydriatic eye drops.

**Diagnosis:** tonometry (IOP), gonioscopy (angle), ophthalmoscopy (optic disc cupping), perimetry (visual fields), OCT.

### Management

**Goal:** lower IOP to a "target" level that stops further optic nerve damage.

**Drugs for open-angle glaucoma (eye drops):**

| Group | Examples | How it lowers IOP | Adverse effects / cautions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Prostaglandin analogues** – usually first choice | **Latanoprost**, travoprost, bimatoprost | ↑ uveoscleral outflow; **once daily at night** | Red eye, **darkening of the iris (brown colour)**, longer darker eyelashes; avoid in pregnancy |
| **Beta-blockers** | **Timolol**, betaxolol | ↓ aqueous production | **Systemic absorption → bronchospasm and slow heart rate; avoid in asthma, COPD, heart block** |
| Alpha-2 agonists | Brimonidine | ↓ production, ↑ outflow | Allergy, dry mouth, fatigue; avoid in infants |
| Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | Dorzolamide, brinzolamide (topical); **acetazolamide** (oral/IV) | ↓ aqueous production | Topical: stinging, bitter taste; oral: tingling, frequent urination, low potassium, kidney stones; sulfonamide allergy |
| Cholinergic (miotics) | **Pilocarpine** | Constricts pupil, opens the angle → ↑ outflow | Small pupil, dim vision, brow ache; mainly in angle-closure |
| Rho-kinase inhibitor | Netarsudil | ↑ trabecular outflow | Red eye |

Fixed combinations (for example timolol + dorzolamide, timolol + brimonidine) reduce the number of drops.

**Acute angle-closure glaucoma (emergency):** lie the patient flat, refer at once; **IV acetazolamide**, **IV mannitol** or oral glycerol (osmotic agents), topical **timolol**, **pilocarpine** (after IOP starts to fall), topical steroid, analgesics and anti-emetics; then **laser peripheral iridotomy** (both eyes usually).

**Surgery and laser:** laser trabeculoplasty (open-angle), trabeculectomy, drainage devices.

**Counselling:** glaucoma needs **lifelong treatment** even without symptoms – stopping drops lets pressure rise silently; use drops at the same time daily; **nasolacrimal occlusion** reduces systemic side effects (important with timolol); wait 5 minutes between drops; tell every doctor you have glaucoma (avoid anticholinergic drugs if angle-closure); regular IOP and visual field checks; screen family members over 40.

## Part B: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR)

## 12.3 Definitions

- **Antimicrobial resistance:** the ability of a microorganism (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) to **survive and grow in the presence of a drug that would normally kill it or stop its growth**, so the drug no longer works.
- **Multidrug-resistant (MDR):** resistant to at least one drug in three or more antimicrobial classes. **Extensively drug-resistant (XDR):** susceptible to only one or two classes. **Pan-drug resistant (PDR):** resistant to all available drugs.
- **Intrinsic resistance:** natural (for example *Pseudomonas* to many drugs, Gram-negatives to vancomycin). **Acquired resistance:** develops by mutation or by gaining resistance genes.

### Important resistant organisms

MRSA (methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), **ESBL**-producing *E. coli* and *Klebsiella*, **carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales** (for example **NDM-1**, New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase), MDR *Acinetobacter* and *Pseudomonas*, **MDR- and XDR-TB**, drug-resistant gonorrhoea, artemisinin-resistant malaria parasites, resistant *Candida auris*, resistant HIV.

## 12.4 Mechanisms of resistance

| Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Enzymatic destruction of the drug** | Beta-lactamases (penicillinase, ESBL, carbapenemases) break beta-lactam antibiotics; aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes |
| **Alteration of the drug target** | Altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) in MRSA; altered DNA gyrase (fluoroquinolones); altered ribosome (macrolides); *rpoB* mutation (rifampicin in TB) |
| **Reduced entry (permeability)** | Loss of porins in Gram-negatives (carbapenems) |
| **Efflux pumps** | Pump the drug out (tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones) |
| **Bypass pathway** | Alternative enzyme not inhibited (sulfonamides, trimethoprim) |

**Spread of resistance genes:** mutation and selection (vertical), and **horizontal gene transfer** between bacteria – **conjugation** (plasmids), transformation (free DNA), transduction (bacteriophage).

```text
Antibiotic use → susceptible bacteria killed
        ↓
Resistant bacteria survive and multiply (selection pressure)
        ↓
Spread: person to person, hospitals, food animals, water, environment
```

## 12.5 Causes of AMR (especially in India)

1. **Overuse and misuse** – antibiotics for viral infections (colds, viral fever, most diarrhoea).
2. **Self-medication and over-the-counter sale** of antibiotics without prescription.
3. Wrong drug, dose or **incomplete courses**; poor-quality or substandard drugs.
4. Irrational fixed-dose combinations and unnecessary broad-spectrum use.
5. **Poor infection control** in hospitals; poor sanitation and hand hygiene in the community.
6. **Antibiotic use in animals and agriculture** (growth promoters, poultry, aquaculture).
7. Pharmaceutical effluents and hospital waste reaching water.
8. Lack of rapid diagnostic tests; few new antibiotics being developed.

## 12.6 Consequences

Longer illness and hospital stay, treatment failure and **more deaths**, need for costlier and more toxic drugs (colistin, carbapenems), risk to surgery, cancer chemotherapy, transplants and neonatal care, and higher health costs – a **global public health threat**.

## 12.7 Prevention and control

### Global and national actions

| Action | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| WHO **Global Action Plan on AMR** | 2015 |
| **One Health approach** | Humans, animals and environment together |
| WHO **AWaRe** classification | **Access** (first-choice, narrow), **Watch** (higher resistance risk – use carefully), **Reserve** (last resort) |
| **Chennai Declaration** | 2012 – Indian medical societies' road map on AMR |
| **Schedule H1** (Drugs Rules) | Introduced 2013 – third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, carbapenems, anti-TB drugs and some others; sold only on prescription, with a **separate register** of prescriber, patient, drug and quantity, kept for 3 years |
| **"Red Line" campaign** | 2016 – a red vertical line on packs of prescription-only antibiotics: "do not use without a prescription" |
| **National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR)** | **2017**, India – awareness, surveillance, infection prevention, rational use, research |
| Surveillance | ICMR AMR surveillance network; national networks |
| Animal sector | India banned colistin for growth promotion in food animals (2019) |

### Antimicrobial stewardship

**Antimicrobial stewardship** is a coordinated programme in a hospital or community that promotes the **appropriate use of antimicrobials** – right drug, dose, route and duration – to improve outcomes and limit resistance. Elements: hospital antibiotic policy, restricted (Reserve) antibiotics needing approval, **culture before antibiotics**, de-escalation to a narrow drug when culture results come, IV-to-oral switch, shortest effective duration, audit and feedback, infection-control team, education.

### Role of the pharmacist

1. **No sale of antibiotics without a valid prescription**; maintain the Schedule H1 register.
2. Counsel to **complete the prescribed course**, take at the right times, and **never share or keep leftover antibiotics**.
3. Explain that antibiotics **do not work on viral infections** (cold, flu, most sore throats).
4. Check dose, duration, interactions and allergies; suggest narrower alternatives where appropriate.
5. Take part in stewardship, prescription audits and adverse drug reaction reporting.
6. Promote **vaccination** (fewer infections → fewer antibiotics), hand hygiene and safe disposal of unused antibiotics.
7. Public awareness – World AMR Awareness Week (November).

### Role of the public

Use antibiotics only when prescribed by a qualified doctor; complete the course; do not demand antibiotics; wash hands; keep vaccinations up to date; prepare food hygienically.

## Remember

- Conjunctivitis: bacterial = purulent, sticky lids → topical antibiotic; viral = watery, pre-auricular node, very contagious → **no antibiotic**, hygiene, lubricants; allergic = itch → antihistamine drops; never self-use steroid drops; red flags = pain, reduced vision.
- Glaucoma: optic nerve damage, IOP normally 10–21 mmHg; POAG silent; acute angle-closure = painful red eye, haloes, vomiting – emergency (acetazolamide, mannitol, pilocarpine, iridotomy).
- Glaucoma drops: latanoprost (iris darkening), timolol (avoid in asthma), brimonidine, dorzolamide, pilocarpine; nasolacrimal occlusion; lifelong use.
- AMR: mechanisms – enzymes, target change, reduced entry, efflux; causes – misuse, OTC sale, animals, poor infection control.
- India: Chennai Declaration 2012, Schedule H1 2013, Red Line 2016, NAP-AMR 2017; WHO GAP 2015; AWaRe; stewardship; pharmacist must not sell antibiotics without prescription.

# Unit 13: Women's health – polycystic ovary syndrome, dysmenorrhoea and premenstrual syndrome

Syllabus chapter 2(m), 4 hours. All three conditions are common in young women, are often managed first in the community, and need sensitive, private counselling. Before studying them, recall the normal menstrual cycle.

## 13.1 The normal menstrual cycle (background)

```text
Hypothalamus → GnRH → Pituitary → FSH and LH → Ovary → oestrogen, progesterone

Day 1–5     Menstruation (shedding of endometrium)
Day 1–14    Follicular phase: FSH → follicle grows → oestrogen rises → endometrium thickens
Day ~14     LH surge → ovulation
Day 15–28   Luteal phase: corpus luteum → progesterone → endometrium ready for implantation
            No pregnancy → corpus luteum regresses → hormones fall → next period
```

A cycle is normally about **21–35 days**; bleeding lasts about 2–7 days.

## 13.2 Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

### Definition

**Polycystic ovary syndrome** is a **common endocrine and metabolic disorder of women of reproductive age**, characterised by a combination of **irregular or absent ovulation**, **excess androgens (male hormones)** and **polycystic-appearing ovaries** on ultrasound, often with **insulin resistance**. It is a leading cause of irregular periods and infertility due to anovulation.

### Diagnostic criteria (Rotterdam criteria – any 2 of 3, after excluding other causes)

1. **Oligo-ovulation or anovulation** – infrequent or absent periods.
2. **Hyperandrogenism** – clinical (excess hair growth, acne, scalp hair thinning) or biochemical (raised testosterone).
3. **Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound** – many small follicles and/or increased ovarian volume.

Other causes to exclude: thyroid disease, high prolactin, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, androgen-secreting tumours.

### Etiopathogenesis

Exact cause unknown; **genetic tendency** + **insulin resistance** + **obesity** and lifestyle.

```text
Insulin resistance → high insulin
        ↓                         ↓
Ovary makes more androgens   Liver makes less SHBG → more free testosterone
        ↓
↑ LH relative to FSH (LH:FSH ratio often raised)
        ↓
Follicles start growing but do not mature → no ovulation → many small cysts
        ↓
Irregular periods, infertility, hirsutism, acne, weight gain
```

### Clinical manifestations

- **Menstrual:** irregular, infrequent or absent periods (oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea); sometimes heavy bleeding.
- **Androgen excess:** **hirsutism** (hair on face, chin, chest, abdomen), **acne**, oily skin, scalp hair thinning.
- **Metabolic:** **weight gain / central obesity**, **acanthosis nigricans** (dark velvety skin on the neck and armpits – a sign of insulin resistance), prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia.
- **Reproductive:** **infertility** (anovulation), higher risk of pregnancy complications (gestational diabetes).
- **Long-term risks:** type 2 diabetes, heart disease, **endometrial hyperplasia and cancer** (unopposed oestrogen from lack of ovulation), sleep apnoea, depression and anxiety.

### Management

Treatment depends on the woman's **main concern** – irregular periods, hirsutism/acne, weight, or wish to conceive.

**Non-drug (first line for everyone, especially overweight women):**
- **Weight loss of even 5–10%** restores ovulation and regular cycles in many.
- Healthy diet (less refined carbohydrate and sugar, more fibre and protein), **regular exercise**, sleep, stress management.
- Cosmetic hair removal (threading, waxing, laser).
- Screening for diabetes, lipids, BP, depression.

**Drug management:**

| Aim | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| **Regular periods, protect endometrium, reduce androgens** (not trying to conceive) | **Combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs)**, for example containing ethinylestradiol with a less androgenic progestin (cyproterone acetate, drospirenone, desogestrel); or **cyclic progestin** (medroxyprogesterone, dydrogesterone) to cause regular withdrawal bleeds |
| **Hirsutism, acne** | COCs first; **anti-androgens** – **spironolactone**, cyproterone, finasteride – **always with reliable contraception** (can feminise a male fetus); topical **eflornithine** for facial hair; acne treatment |
| **Insulin resistance, weight, metabolic risk** | **Metformin** (improves insulin sensitivity, may help cycles); weight-loss medicines in selected patients |
| **Infertility (ovulation induction)** | **Letrozole** (now often first choice) or **clomiphene citrate**; metformin as an add-on; gonadotropins, laparoscopic ovarian drilling or IVF under specialists |

**Counselling:** PCOS is common and manageable, not a cancer; lifestyle change is the most powerful treatment; take the pill daily and know the rule for missed pills; results on hair growth take **6 months or more**; metformin with meals (GI upset at first); pregnancy is possible with treatment; regular check-ups for sugar and lipids.

## 13.3 Dysmenorrhoea

### Definition

**Dysmenorrhoea** is **painful menstruation** – crampy lower abdominal pain occurring just before or during menstrual periods, severe enough to interfere with daily activities.

### Types

| Feature | **Primary dysmenorrhoea** | **Secondary dysmenorrhoea** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | **No pelvic disease**; excess prostaglandins | **Underlying pelvic disease** – endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, copper IUD |
| Age of onset | Within 6–12 months of menarche (when ovulatory cycles begin); teens and early twenties | Usually later (after 25), or a change in the pattern of pain |
| Timing of pain | Starts a few hours before or with bleeding; lasts 1–3 days | May start days before the period and continue after; may have pain with intercourse, heavy or irregular bleeding |
| Examination | Normal | Abnormal findings may be present |

### Etiopathogenesis (primary)

```text
Progesterone falls before menstruation
        ↓
Endometrium releases prostaglandins (PGF2α, PGE2) and leukotrienes
        ↓
Strong, frequent uterine contractions + vasoconstriction → uterine ischaemia
        ↓
Cramping pain; prostaglandins also reach the blood →
nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, dizziness
```

**Risk factors:** young age, early menarche, heavy or long periods, smoking, family history, stress; less common after childbirth.

### Clinical manifestations

Cramping, spasmodic pain in the **lower abdomen**, may spread to the **lower back and thighs**, beginning with the period; nausea, vomiting, loose stools, tiredness, headache, fainting in severe cases.

**Refer** if pain is severe or worsening, not relieved by NSAIDs, started after age 25, is associated with heavy or irregular bleeding, fever, abnormal discharge or pain on intercourse (possible secondary cause).

### Management

**Non-drug:**
- **Local heat** (hot water bottle or heat pad on the lower abdomen) – as effective as some pain-killers.
- Regular **exercise**, yoga and stretching; adequate rest and sleep.
- Stop smoking; balanced diet; reduce caffeine and salt.
- TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) in some.

**Drugs (primary dysmenorrhoea):**

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **NSAIDs** – first choice | **Mefenamic acid**, ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac – reduce prostaglandin production; **start at the first sign of pain or bleeding (or a day before if periods are predictable) and take regularly for 2–3 days**; take with food; avoid in peptic ulcer, kidney disease, aspirin-sensitive asthma |
| Paracetamol | If NSAIDs are not suitable; less effective |
| Antispasmodics | Drotaverine, dicyclomine (often combined with NSAIDs in India) |
| **Hormonal contraceptives** | **Combined oral contraceptive pill**, progestin-only methods or levonorgestrel IUD – suppress ovulation and thin the endometrium → less prostaglandin; useful when contraception is also wanted or NSAIDs fail |

**Secondary dysmenorrhoea:** treat the cause (endometriosis – NSAIDs, hormonal therapy, surgery; PID – antibiotics; fibroids – medical or surgical treatment).

**Counselling:** take the NSAID early and regularly for the first days rather than waiting for severe pain; take with food; heat and exercise help; see a doctor if pain is unusual or not relieved.

## 13.4 Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)

### Definition

**Premenstrual syndrome** is a group of **physical, emotional and behavioural symptoms** that occur **regularly in the luteal phase** (the 1–2 weeks before menstruation) and **resolve within a few days after the period starts**, with a symptom-free interval, severe enough to affect daily life. A severe form with marked mood symptoms is **premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)**.

### Etiopathogenesis

Not fully understood. It is linked to **ovulation**: normal cyclical changes in oestrogen and progesterone trigger an **abnormal response** in sensitive women, especially through altered **serotonin** activity and GABA sensitivity to progesterone metabolites; stress, family history, smoking, lack of exercise and diet may contribute. (Symptoms disappear when ovulation is suppressed, in pregnancy and after menopause.)

### Clinical manifestations

| Emotional / behavioural | Physical |
| --- | --- |
| Irritability, anger, mood swings | **Breast tenderness and swelling** |
| Depressed mood, tearfulness | **Bloating**, fluid retention, weight gain |
| Anxiety, tension | Headache, backache, joint and muscle pain |
| Poor concentration, forgetfulness | Fatigue, sleep change |
| Food cravings, appetite change | Acne flares |
| Social withdrawal | — |

**Diagnosis:** a **prospective symptom diary for at least two cycles** showing symptoms limited to the luteal phase; exclude depression, anxiety disorders and thyroid disease (which do not clear after the period).

### Management

**Non-drug (first line for mild to moderate PMS):**
- **Symptom diary**; education and reassurance.
- **Regular aerobic exercise**; adequate sleep; stress reduction (yoga, relaxation, CBT).
- Diet: small frequent meals, complex carbohydrates, less salt (bloating), less caffeine, alcohol and sugar.
- **Calcium** supplementation has evidence for reducing symptoms; vitamin B6 and magnesium are sometimes used (avoid high-dose B6 – nerve damage).

**Drug management (moderate–severe PMS and PMDD):**

| Drug | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **SSRIs** (fluoxetine, sertraline, escitalopram, paroxetine) | **First-line drugs for PMDD and severe emotional symptoms**; can be taken **daily or only during the luteal phase** (they work faster here than in depression) |
| **Combined oral contraceptives** – especially those containing **drospirenone** | Suppress ovulation → reduce cyclical symptoms |
| **NSAIDs** (mefenamic acid, naproxen) | Pain, headache, breast pain |
| **Spironolactone** | Bloating and breast tenderness (fluid retention) in the luteal phase |
| GnRH analogues (with add-back hormone therapy) | Severe resistant cases; specialist |
| Anxiolytics | Benzodiazepines are generally avoided (dependence) |

**Counselling:** keep a diary to plan ahead; exercise regularly and reduce salt and caffeine before periods; SSRIs may be used only in the second half of the cycle if advised; the pill should be taken daily; seek help if mood symptoms are severe or include thoughts of self-harm.

## 13.5 Comparison of the three conditions

| Feature | PCOS | Primary dysmenorrhoea | PMS / PMDD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main problem | Anovulation + androgen excess + insulin resistance | Painful periods | Cyclical mood and physical symptoms before periods |
| Key mediator | Insulin, androgens, LH | **Prostaglandins** | Hormone-sensitive serotonin activity |
| Timing | Persistent | During first 1–3 days of period | Luteal phase, clears after period starts |
| First-line measure | Weight loss, exercise | NSAIDs (mefenamic acid) + heat | Lifestyle; SSRIs for severe |
| Hormonal option | COC, cyclic progestin | COC | COC with drospirenone |
| Other key drugs | Metformin, spironolactone, letrozole/clomiphene | Antispasmodics | Calcium, NSAIDs, spironolactone |

## Remember

- PCOS: Rotterdam – any 2 of anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries; insulin resistance; lifestyle first; COCs for cycles and hirsutism; metformin; letrozole/clomiphene for fertility; anti-androgens only with contraception.
- Dysmenorrhoea: primary = prostaglandins, no pelvic disease; NSAIDs started early + heat; COCs; investigate secondary causes (endometriosis, fibroids, PID).
- PMS: luteal-phase symptoms that clear after menses; diary for 2 cycles; exercise, diet, calcium; SSRIs (continuous or luteal) for PMDD; drospirenone COC.
